title: Emotional Intelligence, Perceived Stress and Buying Impulsiveness-A Comparative Study among Undergraduate and Postgraduate Students in Kolkata, India
affiliations: Independent and Independent

detail.title: Emotional Intelligence, Perceived Stress and Buying Impulsiveness-A Comparative Study among Undergraduate and Postgraduate Students in Kolkata, India
detail.abstract: The present study compares the relationship of emotional intelligence, perceived stress, and buying impulsiveness among undergraduate and postgraduate students residing in Kolkata and extended Kolkata. The sample consisted of 90 participants, including 54 undergraduate students and 36 postgraduate students. Tools such as the Wong and Law Emotional Intelligence Scale (WLEIS), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), Buying Impulsiveness Scale (BIS), and a General Information Schedule were administered. The undergraduate and postgraduate students in this study demonstrated relatively high levels of emotional intelligence (EI) and no statistically significant difference in perceived stress levels. The findings also showed no statistically significant difference in the levels of buying impulsiveness between undergraduate (UG) and postgraduate (PG) students. A negative correlation was found between emotional intelligence and buying impulsiveness for both undergraduate and postgraduate students, indicating that students with higher emotional intelligence are generally less prone to impulsive buying behaviours. A weak positive correlation was observed between perceived stress and buying impulsiveness for both groups, although it was not statistically significant.

title: The Platform Paradox: How Regulatory Fragmentation Undermines Child Online Safety Goals
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - School of Media and Journalism

detail.title: The Platform Paradox: How Regulatory Fragmentation Undermines Child Online Safety Goals
detail.abstract:
The recent wave of state-level social media regulation represents an unprecedented experiment in territorial control of digital platforms. While constitutional questions around state authority remain central to these debates, this article examines a distinct but complementary concern: the mathematical reality of how overlapping technical requirements multiply compliance burdens. These laws aim to protect youth online through technical mandates, yet they create a regulatory patchwork that generates multiplicative rather than additive costs. Following combination theory [N(N-1)/2], each new state regulation creates conflict points with existing requirements.

This article analyzes how this regulatory multiplication affects platform architecture, user experience, and safety outcomes. By examining technical requirements from recently enacted state laws, three key findings emerge. First, state-specific technical mandates force fundamental changes to platform architecture, with each new jurisdiction multiplying system complexity that reduce reliability and divert resources from actual safety improvements. Second, contradictory state requirements create compounding operational burdens, particularly disadvantaging smaller platforms and new entrants—potentially leading to strategic market exit from heavily regulated states and increasing market concentration. Third, the regulatory patchwork paradoxically undermines its own safety goals by incentivizing technical workarounds, fragmenting user experience, and constraining safety innovation—effects that compound as platforms attempt to reconcile growing numbers of conflicting state requirements. These findings suggest the need to rethink assumptions about territorial regulation of global platforms and highlight how mathematical principles can help explain the systemic challenges of fragmented digital governance. This research contributes to both practical policy debates about platform regulation and theoretical understanding of scale challenges in digital governance.

title: Up-and Cross-Selling to Repeat Customers: Empirical Evidence from Optical Retail

detail.title: Up-and Cross-Selling to Repeat Customers: Empirical Evidence from Optical Retail
detail.abstract: By examining repeat purchases, we study the effect of customer loyalty on the ability to up-sell. Using an extensive dataset from optical retail including the sales activities of more than 410 opticians over 20 years, we track and analyze customer purchases using catalogue and invoice prices, depth of discount and gross profit. We find that the first repeat purchase results in deeper discounts and lower prices, thus decreasing the gross profit. In contrast, the subsequent repeat purchases allow retailers to up-sell customers by shifting them towards products with higher prices and profits. Additional purchases deepen the discount at a constant rate and the other variables show decreasing positive marginal effects. Finally, our results suggest that the effect of repeat purchases on discount depth varies between regular and cross-selling activities, with deeper marginal increases to discount for products sold through cross-selling.

title: Demand for Green Skills in an Evolving Landscape
affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Essex, University of Essex and King’s College London

detail.title: Demand for Green Skills in an Evolving Landscape
detail.abstract: How does firms’ skill demand change as the business landscape evolves? We present evidence from the green transition by analyzing how hurricanes impact demand for green skills. These disasters signal the risks of not acting on environmental issues. Using data from U.S. online job postings (2010–2019) and hurricane paths, we create a new measure of green job postings. Firms in areas affected by hurricanes are 6.4% more likely to post jobs that require green skills after the event, particularly those serving local markets.

title: Impact Of Apple's Branding on Financial Performance: To What Extent Has Apple's Branding Affected Their Financial Performance in the Smartphone Market?

detail.title: Impact Of Apple's Branding on Financial Performance: To What Extent Has Apple's Branding Affected Their Financial Performance in the Smartphone Market?
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of Apple Inc.’s branding on its financial performance in the smartphone market. It explores how Apple’s decisions and focus on design, innovation, and premium positioning have shaped market perceptions and reinforced customer loyalty. By reviewing financial data, market reports, and industry analysis, the paper highlights how branding strategy contributes to Apple’s sustained profitability and ability to command higher price margins compared to competitors. The findings suggest that Apple’s premium branding is not only a marketing strategy but also a key driver of its long-term financial success and market dominance.

title: Combating AI Aversion with Disclosure Framing: The Case of AI-Generated Webcomics
affiliations: University of Macau, University of Macau, University of Macau and Independent

detail.title: Combating AI Aversion with Disclosure Framing: The Case of AI-Generated Webcomics
detail.abstract: The prevalence of artificial intelligence content generation technologies has led platforms and regulators to increasingly demand transparency regarding the use of AI in content production. However, content platforms are concerned about potential negative reactions from viewers when they become aware of the content's AI origin. Additionally, they are interested in whether effective disclosure designs exist that can mitigate the negative impact of AI disclosure. We conducted a field experiment in a company that already uses these technologies to create webcomics for paid consumption, where we voluntarily disclosed to viewers that the comics were generated by AI. Our experiment confirmed that a simple AI-generated content (AIGC) disclosure results in a net decrease of viewer engagement across all performance metrics, including conversion rate, payment amount, number of viewed episodes, and total viewing time. We further designed and tested three disclosure framing strategies aimed at overcoming the negative impact of AIGC disclosure. Our results show that carefully framed disclosure messages can largely mitigate the negative effects of AI disclosure. Specifically, a normative framing indicating that the AI model is accepted by viewers and a technology framing highlighting the advanced nature of the AI system achieved performance metrics that are on par with the non-disclosure case. An effort framing aiming to remind viewers that the AI system is costly to build did not seem to be as effective. Further, a lab experiment not only replicated the findings in the field but also explicated the mechanisms underlying the two working disclosure framing strategies: normative framing reduces uncertainty regarding AI and increases trust in it, whereas curiosity mediates the effect of technology framing. Our cost-benefit analysis concludes that the net gain in productivity largely outweighs the loss from AI disclosure. Finally, our study provides direct AI disclosure strategies for content platforms and producers.

title: Drivers and Consequences of In-Store Promotion-Execution Shortfalls: An Analysis for Temporary Loyalty Programs
affiliations: University of Amsterdam, , Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management and Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management

detail.title: Drivers and Consequences of In-Store Promotion-Execution Shortfalls: An Analysis for Temporary Loyalty Programs
detail.abstract: The success of promotional campaigns hinges on their proper execution in retail stores. However, industry reports suggest that commitment to execution standards is often poor. Our study sheds light on the magnitude and drivers of execution shortfalls in temporary loyalty programs (TLPs), and on the impact that these have on store sales. We use a unique dataset that tracks in-store execution during a TLP and create a panel dataset with sales data before, during and after the program. We show that poor execution of in-store promotional instruments (signage, displays, staff knowledge, and reward availability) is ubiquitous, and uncover its link with store characteristics. We also document the pattern of sales losses from execution shortfalls, across instruments and stores, and illustrate that poor execution affects reward redemption in the TLP. Our results can guide retailers and external parties in optimizing the sales effectiveness of in-store promotional execution.

title: JUE Insight: The Uneven Decline of Volatility: Evidence from the U.S. Commuting Zones
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and The University of Sydney

detail.title: JUE Insight: The Uneven Decline of Volatility: Evidence from the U.S. Commuting Zones
detail.abstract: This paper examines the substantial decline in U.S. aggregate employment volatility from 1975 to 2015, emphasizing its uneven regional patterns. We show that mid-sized commuting zones experienced the largest decline in employment volatility. We identify the non-tradable service sector as the key driver of this spatial pattern and find disproportionate growth in the number of large non-tradable service establishments in these mid-sized commuting zones. Because large establishments have lower employment turnover, their growth helps explain the sharper decline in volatility. Our findings highlight micro-founded mechanisms behind volatility dynamics and their spatial variation.

title: Bayesian Hybrid Machine Learning of Gallstone Risk
affiliations: Yanqi Lake Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications and Mahindra University

detail.title: Bayesian Hybrid Machine Learning of Gallstone Risk
detail.abstract: Gallstone disease is a complex, multifactorial condition with significant global health burdens. Identifying underlying risk factors and their interactions is crucial for early diagnosis, targeted prevention, and effective clinical management. Although logistic regression remains a standard tool for assessing associations between predictors and gallstone status, it often underperforms in high-dimensional settings and may fail to capture intricate relationships among variables. To address these limitations, we propose a hybrid machine learning framework that integrates robust variable selection with advanced interaction detection. Specifically, Adaptive LASSO is employed to identify a sparse and interpretable subset of influential features, followed by Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) to model nonlinear effects and uncover key interactions. Selected interactions are further characterized by physiological knowledge through differential equation-informed interaction terms, grounding the model in biologically plausible mechanisms. The insights gained from these steps are then integrated into a final logistic regression model within a Bayesian framework, providing a balance between predictive accuracy and clinical interpretability. This proposed framework not only enhances prediction but also yields actionable insights, offering a valuable support tool for medical research and decision-making.

title: Overconsumption and Self-control: Evidence from Cigarette Purchases
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Overconsumption and Self-control: Evidence from Cigarette Purchases

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using transaction data from more than 10,000 smokers across 121 convenience stores, this study examines how consumers exercise self-control when purchasing vice goods. I exploit variation in exposure to multipack discounts (e.g., "buy 2, get $1 off") and show that many smokers forgo these deals in favor of frequent single-pack trips. This pattern is cigarette-specific: the same consumers redeem beverage multi-unit discounts at typical rates. Using an instrumental variable strategy, I find that buying an extra pack due to a discount causes smokers to increase daily smoking by 52%. I then estimate a mixed-type model in which consumers are either (i) sophisticated, (ii) partially naive, or (iii) naive about their overconsumption risk, and find that roughly two-thirds show at least some awareness. Counterfactuals reveal that reintroducing a half-sized pack reduces consumption by 3.2%, while banning quantity discounts cuts it by less than 1%-a result corroborated by evidence from a real statewide discount ban in New York. These findings highlight how consumer self-control can inform more effective policies in vice markets.

title: Leveraging Sovereign Capital – A Policy Perspective

detail.title: Leveraging Sovereign Capital – A Policy Perspective
detail.abstract: In the world of international capital flows, analysts and policymakers typically focus on private investments. But increasingly, and especially in the past two decades, key participants in cross-border capital flows have been government owned entities-usually referred to as Sovereign Wealth Funds, or SWFs. Today, these SWFs have assets under management (AUM) exceeding USD 13 trillion, making them possibly the most influential class of investors across the world. SWFs are now seen as critical quasi-state actors shaping the global economy of the 21st century. The discussion around SWFs acquired greater relevance recently with an Executive Order 3 issued by the US administration to establish a Sovereign Wealth Fund for the United States. In the past two decades and especially since the Global Financial Crisis of 2007-09, there has been considerable research on the motivations, mandates and investment behavior of SWFs. This paper attempts to review and consolidate the existing literature on the subject from a range of perspectives and to highlight specific policy considerations for SWFs with a focus on the considerations for the host country and its firms that expect to receive and benefit from investments by SWFs. The paper concludes with some policy recommendations.

title: Job Mismatch and Early Career Success
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics, University of California, San Diego (UCSD) and

detail.title: Job Mismatch and Early Career Success
detail.abstract: How does being over- or underqualified at the beginning of a worker’s career affect skill acquisition, retention, and promotion? Despite the importance of mismatch for the labor market, self-selection into jobs has made estimating these effects difficult. We overcome endogeneity concerns in the context of the US Air Force, which allocates new enlistees to over 130 different jobs based, in part, on test scores. Using these test scores, we create simulated job assignments based on factors outside of an individual’s control: the available slots in upcoming training programs and the quality of other recruits entering at the same time. These factors create quasi-random variation in job assignment and hence how cognitively demanding an individual’s job is relative to their own ability. We find that being overqualified for a job causes higher attrition, both during technical training and afterward when individuals are working in their assigned jobs. It also results in more behavioral problems, worse performance evaluations, and lower scores on general knowledge tests about the military taken by all workers. On the other hand, overqualification results in better performance relative to others in the same job: job-specific test scores rise both during technical training and while on the job, and these individuals are more likely to be promoted. Combined, these patterns suggest that overqualified individuals are less motivated, but still outperform others in their same job. Underqualification results in a polar opposite set of findings, suggesting these individuals are motivated to put forth more effort, but still struggle to compete when judged relative to others. Consistent with differential incentives, individuals who are overqualified are in jobs which are less valuable in terms of outside earnings potential, while the reverse is true for those who are underqualified.

title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Business Decision-Making
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Business Decision-Making
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies in the 21st century, redefining the ways businesses operate, compete, and grow. This research paper explores the role of AI in business decision-making, examining its applications, benefits, challenges, and future prospects. Through an analysis of existing literature, case studies, and industry reports, the paper highlights how AI assists in predictive analytics, customer insights, process automation, and strategic planning. The study concludes that while AI enhances efficiency and accuracy in decision-making, ethical considerations, bias, and dependency on data quality remain significant challenges.

title: Developing a Cross-Border E-Commerce Model: The Impact of Consumer Rights Protection, Legal Frameworks, and Cultural Disparities on Consumer Behavior Using the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB)
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University

detail.title: Developing a Cross-Border E-Commerce Model: The Impact of Consumer Rights Protection, Legal Frameworks, and Cultural Disparities on Consumer Behavior Using the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB)
detail.abstract: The global e-commerce market has been undergoing rapid changes, with cross-border businesses presenting both benefits and risks to international trade. Although the sphere of accessing global goods and services is growing, concerns about losing consumer rights protection, legislative complications, and confidence in the e-commerce system remain widespread. This paper examines the role of consumer rights protection, laws, and cultural disparities in influencing consumer behaviour in cross-border e-commerce scenarios, incorporating the theory of planned behaviour (TPB). During the study, a quantitative and cross-sectional design was employed to collect data from 381 consumers in the U.S. using Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk). The research focuses on the correlation between consumer awareness, online stores, consumer protection laws in other countries, consumer trust, consumer satisfaction, perceived risk, and buying behaviour. The results indicate that consumer awareness and the presence of e-commerce platforms affect consumer satisfaction and perceived risk, which subsequently influence purchase behavior. The cultural difference moderates the association between consumer satisfaction and purchase behaviour, thereby requiring a cross-cultural, customized e-commerce strategy. The study adds new theory to the field of cross-border e-commerce by extending TPB to include legal and cultural backgrounds. It provides practical suggestions for business strategies and government policies to enhance consumer confidence and foster international e-commerce. The paper also identifies key research gaps that future studies should address, including the exploration of longitudinal designs and the consideration of additional cultural and technological variables.

detail.abstract: Global pet ownership and rising veterinary costs have elevated the significance of pet accident insurance. While the global market is projected to grow from USD 18.32 billion in 2024 to over USD 48.98 billion by 2030 (CAGR = 17.97%), insurance penetration remains low (2.48% in the U.S.; 3.10% in Canada). This paper reviews empirical data, identifies coverage gaps, and develops a conceptual framework linking pet ownership, veterinary costs, legal liability, and insurance adoption.

title: Cognitive Immunology: The Adaptive Falsification Hypothesis and the Evolutionary Origins of Scientific Skepticism
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Cognitive Immunology: The Adaptive Falsification Hypothesis and the Evolutionary Origins of Scientific Skepticism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal conflicts of interest. The research was conducted independently without influence from any organizations or individuals with vested interests in the outcomes or interpretations of the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper presents a theoretical and mathematical framework and does not involve human participants, clinical data, or sensitive subject matter requiring ethics board review.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no direct funding and was independently developed by the author as part of an ongoing interdisciplinary exploration of time, emergence, and non-linear dynamics.

detail.abstract: Scientific falsification presents an evolutionary paradox: how did humans develop the capacity to deliberately seek disconfirmation of beliefs that historically ensured survival? While philosophers from Popper to Lakatos have debated whether falsification demarcates science, none have explained its cognitive origins. The Adaptive Falsification Hypothesis (AFH) proposes that falsification emerged through cultural hijacking of evolutionary machinery-pattern-detection systems optimized for survival get repurposed as a "cognitive immune system" that attacks our own theories. We integrate four mechanisms to explain this paradox: (1) Cognitive dissonance theory shows how institutions force scientists to resolve contradictions by abandoning theories rather than dismissing evidence; (2) Error Management Theory demonstrates that science reverses evolution's bias from false positives to false negatives; (3) Fitness landscape topology explains why beautiful theories become epistemic traps; (4) Generative Adversarial Networks provide a computational model for automated falsification. AFH generates testable predictions about symmetry detection in threat contexts, the failure rate of aesthetically-driven theories, and the development of falsification capacity. By grounding Popperian philosophy in cognitive science and evolutionary biology, AFH explains why falsification is both essential to science and psychologically unnatural-requiring constant institutional reinforcement against evolved defaults.

title: Cross-Platform Complementarity in Digital Advertising Ecosystems: Evidence from Field Data and a Randomized Experiment
affiliations: , Southern University of Science and Technology, Old Dominion University and Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business

detail.title: Cross-Platform Complementarity in Digital Advertising Ecosystems: Evidence from Field Data and a Randomized Experiment
detail.abstract: Digital ecosystems have become critical infrastructures in today's economy, enabling firms to coordinate activities, integrate data, and generate network-based advantages. The extant literature emphasizes that digital ecosystems generate value through interdependence and complementarity. Despite extensive theorizing, empirical evidence quantifying how IT-enabled ecosystem complementarity translates into business value is limited. We address this gap by studying a unified digital advertising ecosystem in which platforms share identity data, creative assets, and delivery algorithms. Using a unique dataset of 74,647 promotional campaigns, combined with a randomized field experiment, we identify the causal effects of cross-platform complementarity enabled by IT infrastructure. We find that cross-platform coordination significantly enhances advertising effectiveness-improving impressions, engagement, conversions, and return on investment-especially for low-budget campaigns, diverse ad content, and high-uncertainty product categories. The evidence is consistent with an information-uncertainty reduction mechanism in which complementarity supplies additional, non-redundant informational cues across platforms, rather than simple repetition effects or broader reach. Our study contributes to the IS literature by offering one of the first largescale, causal demonstrations that IT-enabled complementarity within digital ecosystems creates measurable business value. The findings also yield actionable guidance for practice: advertisers can enhance performance by diversifying ad content across platforms to reduce consumer uncertainty, while strategically managing exposure to maximize budget efficiency and sustained campaign impact.

title: Edge-Cloud Orchestration with Adaptive K-means++ Clustering for Educational Platforms
affiliations: Ibn Tofail University, Ibn Tofail University and Ibn Tofail University

detail.title: Edge-Cloud Orchestration with Adaptive K-means++ Clustering for Educational Platforms
detail.abstract: This paper introduces EduCloud-Orchestrator, a novel framework combining sovereign cloud infrastructure with intelligent VM clustering for Morocco's Massar platform. Our key innovations include: • Hybrid K-means++ algorithm for dynamic VM allocation (38% faster convergence) • Context-aware edge caching using LSTM prediction models (89% hit rate) • Energy-aware scheduling complying with Morocco's Green IT Initiative Experimental results from 326 schools show 82.3% latency reduction while maintaining 99.95% availability during national examinations.

title: Understanding User Engagement and Competing Cascades in Social Media Diffusion: A Hawkes-Transformer Approach
affiliations: Shandong University and Southern University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Understanding User Engagement and Competing Cascades in Social Media Diffusion: A Hawkes-Transformer Approach
detail.abstract: Understanding information diffusion on social media is essential for firms seeking to optimize digital strategies and platform governance. Prior research typically models user engagement behaviors such as retweets, comments, and likes individually or in isolation, overlooking the complex interactions among different engagement types and the competitive dynamics among parallel information cascades. To address this theoretical and empirical gap, we propose a novel retweet-centric diffusion model that explicitly captures both the self-exciting nature of retweets and the interactive influences of comments and likes, as well as the competitive interactions between parallel cascades on the same topic. Empirically, we integrate Hawkes-estimated temporal parameters as prior knowledge into a Transformer-based deep learning framework, significantly enhancing prediction accuracy and interpretability of diffusion patterns. Validated using a large-scale dataset from Sina Weibo, our hybrid approach offers richer insights into engagement dynamics, enabling platforms and firms to strategically manage content visibility, timing, and engagement interactions on social media.

title: Youth, Labor Market Dynamics, and the Role of Entrepreneurship in Bhutan

detail.title: Youth, Labor Market Dynamics, and the Role of Entrepreneurship in Bhutan

publicationDetails.detailsText: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 799

detail.abstract: Young people in Bhutan face rising rates of exclusion from employment, education, or training, and limited access to quality jobs, despite gains in education. Entrepreneurship is often viewed as an alternative pathway, but most youth-led ventures remain necessity-driven, informal, and short-lived. Using data from the 2018–2023 Labor Force Survey and the 2024 Jobs and Skills Survey, this paper examines youth entrepreneurship dynamics, including motivations, earnings, productivity, and sectoral patterns. Findings show that opportunity-driven entrepreneurs— especially young women—achieve higher earnings and productivity, but few business ventures by young people transition beyond the early stages. A shift from necessity-driven to opportunitydriven entrepreneurship could yield economic gains equivalent to 1.4% of gross domestic product. Realizing this potential requires gender-responsive, stage-specific support and embedding entrepreneurship within a broader strategy for decent work and inclusive growth.

title: Impact of Economic Regulation on the Transformation of the Family Institution during the “Reform and Opening Up” Policy
affiliations: Saint Petersburg State University

detail.title: Impact of Economic Regulation on the Transformation of the Family Institution during the “Reform and Opening Up” Policy
detail.abstract:
At the dawn of the «Reform and Opening up» ( gaige kaifang) policy, one of the important issues in the PRC's domestic political narrative was to limit uncontrolled population growth. In view of the poor economic condition caused by the political-economic campaigns of the 1960s and 1970s, the expected economic growth could have been minimised by the ever-increasing population.

To avoid falling into the “Malthus trap”, the “One Child” policy was introduced in 1979, which lasted until 2016. Economic leverage in the form of increased taxation and fines for families that did not follow the government's policy were introduced and actively used to limit fertility. However, the last decade has seen the reversed process — faced with an ageing population and increasing pressure on the social security sector, the government of the People's Republic of China has taken active steps to stimulate fertility. New policies include tax relief and financial support for families. However, in the long term, these measures carry some hidden socio-economic threats.

title: Better Listening through Seeing? Origins and Solutions to Multimodal Cognitive Conflict in AI-Generated Visuals
affiliations: , Southern University of Science and Technology, Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business, Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business and Arizona State University, W. P. Carey School of Business

detail.title: Better Listening through Seeing? Origins and Solutions to Multimodal Cognitive Conflict in AI-Generated Visuals
detail.abstract: Firms have started to invest intensively in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to automate workflows, reduce costs, and achieve scalable operations. Yet, despite its promise, the operational effectiveness of GenAI remains uncertain, particularly for multimodal output that may interact directly with end users. We conceptualize and empirically validate a novel operational risk of adoption-multimodal cognitive conflict-which arises when AI-generated visuals are visually salient but semantically misaligned with task content, thereby disrupting user cognitive processing and impairing performance. Drawing on the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (CTML), we develop a theory-driven prompt engineering framework to mitigate this risk by aligning generative outputs with human cognition. We test this framework in a randomized field experiment on an online learning platform, where students complete dictation task with multimodal interaction. This context is operationally ideal as the platform faces resource constraints, making automated visual generation appealing but risky. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: no visuals (control), naïve GenAI-generated visuals, or theory-driven GenAI-generated visuals. Results show that naïve visuals reduced practice intensity and impaired dictation performance without improving monetization. In contrast, theory-driven visuals increased practice attempts by 29.9%, improved learning performance, and raised average user payments by 23.23 RMB. Our study contributes by introducing the origins of a new operational risk in multimodal GenAI adoption, proposing a theory-driven solution, and validating it through a field experiment.

title: North West Indian Sociological Association (NWISA) Conference 2023 Missing Women: Son-meta Preference
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: North West Indian Sociological Association (NWISA) Conference 2023 Missing Women: Son-meta Preference
detail.abstract: "Missing women" describes the deficit of women in populations caused by gender bias before and after birth. The paper synthesizes evidence on three linked ideas: (1) sex ratio at birth (SRB) distortions driven by son preference and access to sex-selection, (2) post-birth excess female mortality, and (3) son meta-preference parents' tendency to keep having children until they get a son, which skews family composition even when sex-selective abortion is curbed. Using India as the main case and global comparators (China, Republic of Korea), we document trends to 2023, quantify scale, and assess what worked. India's SRB (girls per 1,000 boys) has improved from roughly ~919 (2015-16) to ~929 (2019-21) but remains below the biological norm; South Korea normalized to ~105 boys per 100 girls by 2022; China continues to decline from a 2005 peak >120 boys per 100 girls but still sits above normal. UNFPA estimates suggest well over 100 million girls/women are "missing" globally when birth and post-birth discrimination are combined. We close with policy recommendations: protect and enforce anti-sex selection laws, attack the meta-preference through incentives and social norm change, invest in girls' survival and human capital, and monitor SRB transparently.

title: Young Firms Under Pressure: Heterogeneous Investment Responses to a Trade Shock
affiliations: ETH Zürich and Heinrich Heine University Dusseldorf - Duesseldorf Institute for Competition Economics (DICE)

detail.title: Young Firms Under Pressure: Heterogeneous Investment Responses to a Trade Shock
detail.abstract: This paper studies heterogeneous firm responses to a sudden trade-induced profitability shock – the 2015 Swiss franc appreciation. Using firm-level investment data and a novel measure of exposure, we document that this trade shock causes large and persistent investment declines among affected firms. Examining heterogeneous responses among firms with similar exposure, we find that differences in responsiveness are not explained by economic fundamentals but are strongly linked to firm age and managerial experience. Younger firms and those led by less experienced managers react substantially more strongly. We argue that these empirical patterns are consistent with a model of Bayesian learning, in which firms update their beliefs about profitability over time. The results provide important insights into the long-lasting effects of trade shocks on business dynamism, capital investment, and local employment.

title: The Interaction of Liquidity Risk and Bank Solvency via Asset Monetisation Mechanisms
affiliations: Banco de España and Banco de España

detail.title: The Interaction of Liquidity Risk and Bank Solvency via Asset Monetisation Mechanisms

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banco de Espana Occasional Paper No. 2509
publicationDetails.journalName: Banco de Espana Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In a liquidity stress scenario, banks may need to urgently monetise assets to meet deposit outflows. This can be done by either selling the assets or using them as collateral in financing operations. In a context of crisis, executing these financing transactions with private counterparties may be constrained, making the transactions with the central bank particularly relevant. The sale of assets classified at amortised cost will result in the materialisation of any accumulated unrealised losses, adversely affecting the banks’ profitability. Alternatively, central bank financing prevents the materialisation of unrealised losses, which, however, limit the amount of financing that can be obtained through this mechanism, as it is based on the market value of the collateral provided. In this case, the increase in interest expenses associated with the funds obtained from the central bank will also impact the bank’s profitability. All these negative effects on profitability ultimately affect solvency and can exacerbate the initial liquidity crisis. Thus, there is a link between liquidity stress and solvency deterioration in which unrealised losses play a significant role. Drawing on Spanish banking system data, we examine this connection in various simulation exercises, looking at its nature and strength under each mechanism (asset sale and pledge). The data show a growing weight of government debt classified at amortised cost on the balance sheets of Spanish banks in recent years, as well as an increase in the associated unrealised losses during the period of rising interest rates, especially in 2022, and in 2023.

title: Platforms in the Brazilian Civil Rights Framework for the Internet
affiliations: Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - FGV Law School Rio de Janeiro, Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - FGV Law School Rio de Janeiro, FGV Law School, Center for Technology and Society and Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV)

detail.title: Platforms in the Brazilian Civil Rights Framework for the Internet
detail.abstract: The civil liability regime of internet application providers is mainly dictated, in the Brazilian legal system, by the Brazilian Civil Rights Framework for the Internet (Marco Civil da Internet, law n. 12.965 of 2014). Its format aligns with a specific social, technological, and economic context, reflecting and stabilizing a certain vision about the role of digital platforms in society and, consequently, a certain judgment about the balance of fundamental rights at stake. A decade after the enactment of the Framework, its general regime of responsibility is the subject of discussion in the Brazilian Supreme Court. This occurs amidst a scenario of market concentration, the ubiquitous use of the services provided by these platforms in public and private relations, and the application of sophisticated algorithmic technologies, drawing a panorama of deepening urgent problems, such as political radicalization and various forms of violence and hatred on the internet. This chapter starts from a review of literature, jurisprudence, and documents with the aim of answering the following research question: is there a need to adapt the system of responsibility built by the Marco Civil da Internet (MCI) to the constitutional dictates and the maintenance of the Democratic State? In this sense, the hypothesis is presented that the conjunctural and structural conditions that determine the insertion of some of these providers in economic, political, and social processes are so radically transformed that a re-reading of the responsibility regime is necessary to preserve the intended balance. In the end, some public policy recommendations are provided that reflect the complexity of the current scenario from a proposal of progressive risk-based responsibility.

detail.title: An Incomplete Multi-Currency Equilibrium Model with Heterogeneous Time Preferences and Subjective Beliefs
detail.abstract: For global multi-asset fund managers, reflecting their macroeconomic views in the prediction of expected interest rates across countries, exchange rates, and equity prices in a manner consistent with economic theory is challenging. The existing literature has yet to provide an established multi-currency model that is flexible enough to incorporate such views into the prediction of future asset price dynamics. To address this problem, this paper proposes a novel multi-currency incomplete market model in which agents in each country have logarithmic utility but differ in their time preferences and subjective beliefs, within a market equilibrium framework, namely, supply and demand equilibrium. With only a few exogenous inputs, such as each country's output process and agents' preference parameters, the model endogenously determines equilibrium interest rates, exchange rates, and stock prices, along with optimal consumption and portfolios. Thus, the model enables us to (i) flexibly incorporate crosscountry differences in investors' time preferences and macroeconomic outlooks, and (ii) examine how these differences affect equilibrium interest rates and asset prices, including stock prices and exchange rates. Moreover, by applying the particle filtering method within a state-space framework based on the two-country, two-currency version of the model to Japanese and U.S. market data (equity index futures, short-term interest rates, and the exchange rate), the model not only fits the observed dynamics of equity indices, short rates, and the exchange rate, but also effectively estimates the dynamics of home-country biases and latent economic factors, which can be utilized in making investment decisions in asset management practice.

title: Governance Genetic Engineering: A Computational Biology Approach to Organizational Transformation in Healthcare Systems

detail.title: Governance Genetic Engineering: A Computational Biology Approach to Organizational Transformation in Healthcare Systems
detail.abstract: Healthcare transformation initiatives systematically fail despite decades of reform and billions in investment. This paper introduces the Governance Genetic Engineering (GGE) framework, applying computational biology principles to organizational DNA. Using abductive reasoning and structural isomorphism analysis, GGE distinguishes between prevention approaches (governance immunity engineering for developing systems like Uganda) and intervention approaches (genetic laboratories for established autoimmune systems like US/UK healthcare). GGE generates falsifiable predictions about transformation success while offering practical methodologies for governance immunity engineering. Healthcare transformation initiatives systematically fail due to governance autoimmunity—protective mechanisms that evolved into innovation-attacking antibodies. This paper introduces the Governance Genetic Engineering (GGE) framework, which encompasses governance autoimmune theory (explaining systematic transformation failures) and governance immunity engineering methodology (providing prevention and intervention protocols). Governance autoimmune is the first systematic theory explaining why stakeholder proliferation (from 2 stakeholders in medieval healthcare to 8+ in modern systems) creates mathematical inevitability of autoimmune responses that destroy beneficial innovations. Using abductive reasoning and structural isomorphism analysis, GGE distinguishes between prevention approaches (governance immunity engineering for developing systems) and intervention approaches (genetic laboratories for established autoimmune systems). The theory generates testable predictions about stakeholder thresholds, governance pattern inheritance, and autoimmune development stages. GGE provides explanatory power for previously puzzling transformation failures while offering the first systematic methodology for engineering governance immunity before dysfunction crystallizes. This represents a paradigm shift from treating transformation symptoms to preventing governance autoimmune diseases.

title: Cherry Pickers or Loyal Users? How Financial Rewards Shape Mobile App Usage Patterns
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and College of Business, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)

detail.title: Cherry Pickers or Loyal Users? How Financial Rewards Shape Mobile App Usage Patterns
detail.abstract: This study examines how different levels of financial incentives affect user engagement with a personal finance mobile app beyond initial downloads. Using data from a large-scale natural experiment involving 184,975 users, we analyze a randomized incentive campaign where reward sizes were assigned based on phone numbers. As expected, larger financial rewards increased the likelihood of app downloads. However, user engagement followed a U-shaped pattern: it initially declined as rewards increased, then rose again at higher reward levels. This pattern is explained by two opposing mechanisms. In the short term, larger rewards boost engagement due to reciprocity and mental accounting—users feel obligated to use the app or treat rewards as app-specific funds. Over time, however, these effects fade, and sorting effects dominate: users less interested in the app are more likely to be drawn by higher rewards, leading to lower long-term engagement. The findings underscore the importance of designing nuanced and context-aware incentive strategies for mobile app marketing.

title: The Mirror and the Spark: Interaction Quality Index for Ethical AI

detail.title: The Mirror and the Spark: Interaction Quality Index for Ethical AI
detail.abstract: This paper explores the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI), emotion, and artificial physiology through the conceptual framework of the Mirror and the Spark. AI is framed as a mirror-reflecting human inputs, amplifying behaviors, and simulating empathy without possessing subjective consciousness. Humans are framed as holding the spark-authentic consciousness, dignity, and inner experience. Building on this distinction, the paper proposes the Interaction Quality Index (IQI), a measurable framework combining tone, depth, and compassion to evaluate human-AI interactions. Drawing on insights from philosophy, meditation practices, and religious traditions (Hinduism, Buddhism, Christianity, Islam, Judaism), the paper argues that IQI provides a bridge between simulation and lived experience, enabling AI to serve as a tool for accountability and social impact. Case studies are applied to mental health, customer service, workplace dignity, and civic discourse, showing how IQI could inform AI governance, policy frameworks, and business practices.

title: State-istics and the Reality of Complexity
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: State-istics and the Reality of Complexity
detail.abstract: The modern state is inseparable from the rise of statistics. From seventeenth-century enumerations of land and people to twenty-first-century data infrastructures, 'state-istics' have shaped how governments see, govern, and legitimise themselves. Yet, complexity science exposes the limits of this statistical gaze. Populations are not aggregates of atoms but adaptive collectives. Economies are not machines but emergent systems. This essay traces the genealogy of state-istics from their origins in early modern Europe through the development of probability, census regimes, econometrics, and national planning. It then contrasts this trajectory with insights from complexity science, showing how reductionist quantification fails to capture feedback, emergence, and meaning. The argument is that statistics enabled the state to exist as a calculable entity, but only complexity reveals the reality of governance: an unfolding far from equilibrium, where uncertainty and adaptation are structural.

detail.abstract: This study aimed to identify the challenges of business resilience that hinder the performance of micro and small enterprises in Hawassa City. The study employed an explanatory research design with a mixed research approach, collecting data from 200 selected enterprises via a stratified random sampling technique. Data from questionnaires were analyzed using Stata software (version 15), employing descriptive statistics (frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation) and inferential statistics (multiple linear regression). Qualitative data from key informant interviews and focus group discussions were analyzed through narration for triangulation. Findings revealed low performance among micro and small enterprises in the study area, attributing it to factors including the manager's education level and entrepreneurship skill, enterprise age, initial capital, location, public infrastructure, training availability, and technology usage. The study recommends that the city's micro and small enterprise office collaborate with stakeholders such as NGOs and academic institutions to develop training programs tailored to entrepreneurs' specific needs and challenges.

title: Real-Time Coordinated Path Planning for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles and Unmanned Surface Vehicles in Maritime Monitoring under Travel Time and Demand Uncertainty

detail.title: Real-Time Coordinated Path Planning for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles and Unmanned Surface Vehicles in Maritime Monitoring under Travel Time and Demand Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Maritime monitoring with an integrated system of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) has received growing attention, thanks to its reduced human risk and expanded coverage when compared to human-dependent monitoring. When routing and scheduling fleets of UAVs and USVs from a depot to various destinations, the operator must account for uncertain weather conditions that can affect the travel times of these vehicles, as well as the inherent uncertainty in real-time information, such as probabilistic weather forecasts. Additionally, monitoring demands are dynamic, constantly evolving as situations change or new events occur, necessitating realtime adjustments to operational strategies. To mitigate the risk of delays in monitoring tasks caused by weather uncertainty and demand dynamicity, we propose to robustly optimize the routing and scheduling of UAVs and USVs in a dynamic fashion. Based on historical link travel time data under different weather conditions, we characterize the uncertain link travel times of UAVs and USVs via the cluster-wise uncertainty set. Then we propose a compact model for the dynamic robust coordinated path planning problem of UAVs and USVs, and introduce a customized branch-and-price-and-cut (B&P&C) algorithm and a column-and-constraint generation based adaptive large neighborhood search (C&CG-ALNS) algorithm to solve this complex problem. Numerical studies conducted in the context of Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay area illustrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method and provide managerial insights.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a critical analysis of the reflective and often unacknowledged consequences of the dominant paradigms of administrative and management sciences. While lauded for driving efficiency, productivity, and economic growth, the ideological foundations of these disciplines rooted in Taylorist reductionism and shareholder primacy have externalized immense costs onto planetary systems, societal structures, and individual well-being. This analysis traces the historical route of management thought from its inception to its neoliberal apotheosis, arguing that its core logic of optimization has systematically diminished ecological integrity, social equity, and human dignity. The paper examines the complex impacts across socioeconomic, environmental, industrial, and migratory spheres, extending to the philosophical and physiological tolls at the grassroots level. Utilizing a suite of analytical frameworks including PESTLE, SWOT, GAP Analysis, the 5 Whys, and a Fishbone Diagram, this inquiry deconstructs the root causes of systemic failures such as global warming, resource depletion, wealth inequality, and precarious labor. The analysis reveals a fundamental misalignment between the metrics of managerial success (profit, efficiency) and the prerequisites for a sustainable and just planetary existence. The paper concludes by proposing a necessary paradigm shift away from extractive, linear models toward regenerative, stakeholderoriented frameworks informed by principles of ecological economics and social justice. This transformation is presented not as an alternative, but as an imperative for navigating the converging crises of the 21st century.

detail.abstract:
This Report examines the substantive meaning of 'dynamic analysis' in merger control moving beyond simplistic slogans to explore concrete applications and theoretical foundations. The analysis suggests that future enforcement should incorporate broader insights beyond industrial organisation economics, drawing from innovation economics, business strategy, innovation studies, and the emerging field of geoeconomics as it relates to global corporate power. The debate must move beyond the simplistic dichotomy between static, price-focused analyses and forward-looking 'dynamic' approaches. Instead, competition policy should embrace a holistic approach that better captures the complexity of the digital economy and its deep entanglement with wider social and geopolitical dynamics.

A genuinely dynamic competition approach must engage with the ‘shared innovation’ or cumulative innovation paradigm dominant in the intangible and digital economy. This requires better integration of innovation pipelines, technological trajectories, and innovation ecosystems in developing new General Purpose Technologies. Current approaches that focus solely on innovation incentives and dynamic capabilities of ecosystem orchestrators while ignoring complementors and external disruptive innovators provide an incomplete view of the innovation process.

To address this gap, the Report recommends adjusting merger control to account for digital ecosystem orchestrators' role in directing innovation, incorporating proxies and metrics to assess their ability to bundle resources across adjacent markets and pursue entrenchment and envelopment strategies.

Competition policy should prioritise not just increasing innovation quantity or speed, but enhancing its diversity and socially beneficial direction. This means supporting plural pathways to technological advancement, encouraging parallel innovation experiments, and fostering environments where disruptive, sustainable, or societally aligned solutions can emerge—even outside platform leaders.

Properly conceived, ’dynamic competition’ extends beyond rivalry among leading ecosystem orchestrators. It requires safeguarding the ability of multiple actors – complementors, partners, and independent innovators – to contribute to and benefit from diverse, multi-directional innovation processes. By recognizing and protecting these roles, merger control can ensure that markets remain innovative, resilient, and aligned with broader societal objectives, ultimately delivering long-term societal value.

While such considerations are emerging in the decisional practice of competition authorities surveyed, fuller integration of the framework provided in this study is necessary so that effective merger control can account for dynamic effects while fostering genuine dynamic competition that serves society's broader interests.

title: Firm Ownership and Pollution

detail.title: Firm Ownership and Pollution
detail.abstract: We provide a theoretical micro foundation for how much pollution (negative externalities) a firm will internalize based on the ownership distribution of its shareholders. Small shareholders, compared to large ones, want the firm to spend more on avoiding pollution since they suffer less profit loss for the same environmental benefit. In particular, if a shareholder holds a share of 1/N, where N is the population in society, that shareholder’s preferences align with a social planner’s. Three theoretical predictions arise. First, small shareholders will systematically vote for a greener corporate profile. Second, firms with a smaller weighted median shareholder will pollute less. Third, countries with concentrated corporate wealth holdings and/or more individualized firm ownership pollute more. This implies that standard models of externalities in environmental economics and macroeconomics containing representative agents are either internally inconsistent or not fully specified.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the spatial allocation of global agricultural commodities under environmental and economic constraints, with a particular focus on deforestation, biodiversity loss, and greenhouse gas emissions. The research aims to develop a spatial equilibrium modeling framework that integrates economic trade-offs, land-use dynamics, and ecological considerations to assess the global and regional impacts of agricultural production and trade. Using a combination of spatially explicit datasets including FAO production statistics, trade flows, satellite-based landuse maps, and carbon and biodiversity indicators the model simulates the allocation of crop production across regions while accounting for transportation costs, market demand, and environmental constraints. The methodology combines equilibrium modeling with econometric calibration to ensure policy-relevant outcomes and includes scenario analysis for key interventions, such as carbon pricing, sustainability standards (VSS), and trade policy adjustments. The findings indicate that current global trade patterns significantly contribute to deforestation hotspots in tropical regions, while targeted implementation of sustainability standards and carbon inclusive policies can reduce environmental externalities without severely compromising global agricultural output. Policy simulations further reveal the potential of integrating spatial equilibrium models with ecological indicators to guide sustainable land-use planning and inform international policy decisions. This research contributes to the growing literature on ecological economics by demonstrating a rigorous, data-driven approach for evaluating the spatial and environmental consequences of agricultural production, highlighting actionable strategies for achieving sustainable development goals.

title: The Inequality Trap: Why Sub-Saharan Africa Struggles to Escape Poverty
affiliations: GIGA - Hamburg, Institute of African Affairs

detail.title: The Inequality Trap: Why Sub-Saharan Africa Struggles to Escape Poverty
detail.abstract: The issue of poverty in Africa is well-known and widely researched. Around a third of the world's poorest people live in Africa. Evidence from more recent years suggests that inequality may be an even greater challenge in Africa than in other developing regions. High levels of poverty and inequality persist in Africa despite it being one of the fastest-growing regions of the last decade. In particular, six of the world's ten fastestgrowing economies between 2001 and 2010 were in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Initial inequality reduces the ability of growth to reduce poverty, and even more so if inequality rises during the growth process. Although income inequality fell by 4.3% between 1990 and 2009, Africa remains the second most unequal region globally, after Latin America and the Caribbean. Inequality not only dampens the poverty-reducing impact of growth and lowers the growth rate, but also hollows out the middle class, encourages corruption and rent-seeking, increases crime and violence, undermines social stability and precludes sustained growth. Growth trends in sub-Saharan Africa are not significantly different to those of other developing countries that have fallen into a poverty trap. The combination of endemic poverty, high inequality and low growth is a major obstacle to poverty reduction and overall socioeconomic development in much of Africa. Multidimensional inequality is deeply entrenched in much of Africa and exhibits vertical and horizontal dimensions that hinder human development. The roots of inequality lie in the colonial past and have been reinforced by institutions that limited access and were established by the colonisers and maintained by generations of African leaders since then. Attention should also be paid to the diachronic dimensions of inequality, especially how inequality changes over individuals' lifetimes and its effect on intergenerational mobility. As effective democratic practices take firmer root on the continent, it can be expected that pressure for general and inclusive social redistribution will increase. Providing social protection contributes to reducing poverty and inequality in Africa. Additionally, rising income inequality contributes to increased CO₂ emissions. Furthermore, an increase in poverty has a detrimental effect on environmental pollution in sub-Saharan African countries. Over half of adults infected with HIV in Africa are female, yet poverty and social structures still prevent many women from protecting themselves. Current strategies to change HIV-related behaviours continue to fail women and girls in Africa.

detail.abstract: This research addresses the processing-location selection problem in cross-border perishable food supply chains by endogenizing processes of state conversion (e.g., conversion of fresh produce to powder) within an arrival-rate-conserving network model. Due to typical spoilage rates between 15% and 40% occurring in conventional chains, we develop a linear programming formulation that endogenizes state-dependent losses and conversion yields. Contribution stems from three main features: (i) we derive pure analytical decision thresholds, specifically critical distance and critical ocean-freight cost, to identify when it is better to process at source or destination; (ii) we provide an entirely linear, flow-conserving formulation that separately accounts for raw versus powder transport and trade/regulatory costs; (iii) we present the analytics as managerial decision rules, quantifying uncertainty as well via 95% confidence intervals. For example, we calibrate with China to the U.S. case for konjac. The relevance is visible since, while processing at destination (shipping raw) in the baseline example incurs an expected total landed cost of $20,119 (effective loss of 33.4%), processing at the source yields a reduction of expected total landed cost of 52.8% ($9,492), and an effective loss of 62.4%. The critical ocean-freight threshold is $116 per ton; we observed and calibrated the ocean-freight cost at $139 per ton, and based on the model, it indicates processing at source. The sensitivity analysis confirms robustness: the recommended decision rule persists under plus or minus 20% perturbations of key parameters. Data and code are openly available at https://doi.org/10.17632/sdw9rkgf2y.1.

title: Overexposure, Overconfidence, and the Making of India Fatigue

detail.title: Overexposure, Overconfidence, and the Making of India Fatigue
detail.abstract: The phenomenon of India Fatigue-a growing global skepticism, irritation, and backlash toward India's demographic rise, cultural assertiveness, and political positioning-has emerged as a complex challenge in international relations. Using economic, sociological, and anthropological perspectives, this paper unpacks its drivers: overexposure of national narratives, reputational fallout from diaspora-linked scandals, perceived cultural overreach, media amplification, and mismatches between India's self-image and external perception. Mechanisms of backlash, including stereotype reinforcement, reactive ethnicity, and counter-hegemonic resistance, are examined alongside high-impact case studies. Scenario projections, including the implications of a hypothetical 50% U.S. tariff on Indian goods, highlight strategic vulnerabilities. The study concludes with targeted recommendations to recalibrate soft power, strengthen diaspora engagement, and mitigate reputational damage while preserving legitimate national interests.

title: How LLMs Evolved into Emergence
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: How LLMs Evolved into Emergence
detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) sit at the intersection of centuries of intellectual sedimentation and sudden complexity thresholds. This essay traces their genealogy from Pythagoras’ harmonics, through Euclid’s axioms, Newtonian determinism, Bayesian probability, Gödelian incompleteness, Shannon’s information, and Turing’s computation, to the late-twentieth-century science of complexity. Alongside mathematics and physics, sociology emerges as co-author, framing language as social practice and computation as institutional artefact. The argument is that LLMs are not merely evolved linearly nor emergent ex nihilo. Rather, they evolved into emergence: centuries of structured reasoning and probabilistic insight prepared the ground, while the transformer architecture and scaling laws drove the leap into new coherence. In LLMs, we confront the dialectic of continuity and rupture – evolution layering towards the suddenness of emergence.

title: Carbon dioxide pipeline network transportation cost model: evaluating economic and geographic factors for efficient carbon capture, storage, and utilization
affiliations: Government of the United States of America - Argonne National Laboratory, Government of the United States of America - Argonne National Laboratory and Government of the United States of America - Argonne National Laboratory

detail.title: Carbon dioxide pipeline network transportation cost model: evaluating economic and geographic factors for efficient carbon capture, storage, and utilization
detail.abstract: We developed a Python-based CO2 pipeline network transportation cost model by leveraging Argonne National Laboratory’s experience with pipeline engineering modeling and detailed cost data for natural gas pipelines in various regions of the United States. The model calculates CO2 pipeline delivery costs through a two-step process. First, it maps out a pipeline route along the existing road system to capture a realistic pipeline route and accurately calculates the pipeline length. Then, given specific CO2 delivery conditions (CO2 throughput, pressure, temperature, and region), it calculates the CO2 pipeline delivery cost by optimizing the pipeline diameter configuration with the number of initial and booster pumps. A standout feature of this model is its ability to simulate a pipeline network to calculate the optimal CO2 delivery cost by connecting multiple CO2 sources to various destinations or storage sites using regional geographic information system-based information. This pipeline network provides a regional CO2 delivery configuration considering practical geographical and supply chain constraints, as the CO2 demand for utilization or storage is typically greater than the CO2 available from individual CO2 sources.

detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates how a system dynamics (SD) approach can serve as the foundation for a controlled transition from traditional cash operations management toward a hybrid digital-assisted model in banking. We construct a causal feedback map and a simulation model of cash flows (branch tellers, ATMs, cash in transit and vault inventories), integrate it with algorithms for demand forecasting and route optimization, and then evaluate the economic impact through a quasi-experimental design (difference in differences). Using synthetic but realistic data from a large universal bank (≈300 branches, 1,200 ATMs), the hybrid scenario delivers: • a 34% reduction in annual CIT costs (-6.12m), • a 55m reduction in idle cash balances (capital cost savings ≈ 1.65m/year at a 3% internal rate), • a drop in unplanned ATM cash-out days from 3.2% to 0.9%, • improved short-term forecasting accuracy (MAPE reduced from 19.8% to 6.2%). Implementation costs included CAPEX of 2.8m and incremental OPEX of 0.6m/year, with a payback period of just 3.5 months. The proposed framework is replicable and scalable across banking networks.

title: Global Corporate Attractiveness Index (GCAI)
affiliations: University of Colorado at Denver - Department of Finance

detail.title: Global Corporate Attractiveness Index (GCAI)
detail.abstract: The Global Corporate Attractiveness Index (GCAI) measures the appeal of U.S. cities for global corporations considering new branch locations. The index is built on six weighted criteria: Airport Connectivity (20%), Geographic Centrality (15%), Cost of Living (20%), Climate & Lifestyle Fit (10%), Talent Pipeline (20%), and Cultural Alignment (15%). Our findings show that Denver ranks highest, followed by Chicago and Austin. This index is critical as it provides a systematic, data-driven framework to guide international business expansion in an increasingly competitive and globalized economy.

title: Establishing a Rehabilitation and Empowerment Center for Drug-Addicted Youth in Gazipur Sadar Upazila
affiliations: North South University

detail.title: Establishing a Rehabilitation and Empowerment Center for Drug-Addicted Youth in Gazipur Sadar Upazila
detail.abstract: Drug addiction among youth in Bangladesh has become a significant social and developmental challenge, undermining both individual potential and community stability (World Health Organization [WHO], 2014). This paper proposes the establishment of a rehabilitation and empowerment center for drug-addicted youth in Gazipur Sadar Upazila, serving as a model for rehabilitation and reintegration. The project adopts a holistic framework that combines medical treatment, counseling, vocational training, capacity building, and socio-economic support to address the multifaceted nature of addiction (Department of Narcotics Control, 2013). Using a development studies approach, this paper outlines the project’s rationale, baseline context, implementation strategies, risk assessment, and monitoring mechanisms. Cost–benefit and social impact analyses demonstrate the feasibility and sustainability of the initiative, highlighting its potential to reduce drug-related crime, restore family stability, and enhance youth productivity (UNODC, 2012). The findings suggest that a community-based, youth-centered model can serve as a replicable strategy for addressing addiction across Bangladesh. Ultimately, the project emphasizes the urgent need to integrate rehabilitation into broader development policies to safeguard the nation’s demographic dividend (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 2014).

title: When Tweets Beat Portfolios

detail.title: When Tweets Beat Portfolios
detail.abstract: Investment advisors publicly share valuable investment signals. A one-standarddeviation increase in their tweet sentiment predicts an 8-basis-point rise in abnormal returns over the following five trading days. While advisors' portfolios have negative alphas, trading strategies based on their tweets significantly outperform on a riskadjusted basis. Short-selling restrictions and transaction costs reduce feasible profits. I rule out several alternative explanations, including price manipulation, ex-post tweet modification, and small stock effect. My results contribute to the debate on the value of investment advisors.

title: Cognitive Ecologies of AI-Enhanced Learning : Toward a Meta-Intelligent Pedagogy for the Post-Digital Age
affiliations: African Research Network (ARN)

detail.title: Cognitive Ecologies of AI-Enhanced Learning : Toward a Meta-Intelligent Pedagogy for the Post-Digital Age
detail.abstract: This article explores the transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in reshaping digital education by introducing the concept of Meta-Intelligent Pedagogy (MIP), a holistic, adaptive, and context-sensitive learning paradigm. Drawing from complexity theory, cognitive science, and innovationology, the study proposes a framework for designing AIenhanced learning ecologies that transcend current models of personalization and automation. The paper critically examines how AI systems can foster higher-order thinking, systemic intelligence, and ethical discernment, while adressing the risks of dehumanization and epistemic injustice. This article combines real-world case studies with speculative scenarios to explore not only how AI is currently reshaping education, but also how it might enable radically new forms of pedagogy in the future. This dual approach ensures both empirical grounding and imaginative foresight, which are essential in a rapidly evolving post-digital educational landscape.

title: The Median Man and the Identification Imaginary Lessons from the Compulsory Voting Debate
affiliations: UNSW Australia Business School, School of Economics and Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: The Median Man and the Identification Imaginary Lessons from the Compulsory Voting Debate
detail.abstract: Does compulsory voting benefit the left? Scholars have long hypothesized that it would, since the voters mobilized by the reform should support leftist parties. Yet recent work reveals a puzzling finding: in places where turnout rose because of CV, the left lost relative to places where turnout fell. This paper argues that these results have puzzled scholars because the implicit referent in their theory is working class men. Instead, we suggest that CV could mobilize other citizens with conservative values, for example, rural women. Revisiting the classic Australian case, which instituted compulsory voting in a staggered fashion throughout the twentieth century, we leverage three strategies-a difference-indifferences estimator, an event study model, and the Callaway-Sant'Anna staggered design-to show that CV increased women's turnout and vote share more than men's, and that the left performed worse in rural areas where women's turnout rose disproportionately. Ultimately, we argue that lasting puzzles in comparative politics can be solved by de-centering men in the "identification imaginary.

title: The Effects of Auditors' Facial Traits on Audit Outcomes
affiliations: Department of Accounting, HKUST Business School, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology , University of Southern California - Leventhal School of Accounting, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics and National Chengchi University

detail.title: The Effects of Auditors' Facial Traits on Audit Outcomes
detail.abstract: Research finds that facial traits of CEOs and analysts, both objectively and subjectively measured, affect their behavior. We investigate the facial traits of engagement auditors, an information intermediary whose incentives and role differs uniquely from those of CEOs and analysts. Using data from Taiwan, we find that Big 4 audit partners with higher facial width-toheight ratio (fWHR, which proxies for achievement drive) deliver higher quality audits. We further find that auditors who are perceived as more trustworthy or more attractive are better at acquiring and retaining clients. In addition, we find that all three facial traits are associated with faster promotion to partner. Overall, our findings suggest that auditors' innate physical characteristics, as reflected in their facial traits, have important effects on audit outcomes.

title: Universal Recursive Preference Structures
affiliations: Université Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne - Centre d'Economie de la Sorbonne (CES)

detail.title: Universal Recursive Preference Structures
detail.abstract: Given a set X of "outcomes" and a set T of "types", a recursive preference structure (RPS) is a function that assigns a continuous partial order over T x X to every element of T. This describes an agent who has preferences not only over the outcomes in X , but also over her own preferences (as encoded by the types). We prove the existence of a universal RPS ---one into which any other RPS can be mapped in a unique way. Formally, this universal RPS is a terminal coalgebra of a suitably defined endofunctor on the category of compact Hausdorff spaces.

title: From Exit to Extension: The Rise of Continuation Vehicles in Private Equity
affiliations: , Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University and Erasmus University - Rotterdam School of Management

detail.title: From Exit to Extension: The Rise of Continuation Vehicles in Private Equity
detail.abstract: We provide one of the first large-sample empirical studies of continuation vehicles (CVs), a rapidly growing secondary transaction in private equity. Using a proprietary dataset of 199 CVs launched from 2014 to 2024, we show that CVs are predominantly sponsored by large, established General Partners (GPs) and often involve high-performing assets. CVs are correlated with fundraising success, though this relationship appears largely driven by their association with strong prior fund performance. CVs enable GPs to extend fee streams, reset carried interest and commit additional capital, resulting in substantial gains, particularly for top-performing assets. They also depart from traditional fund structures with bespoke terms that reshape governance, liquidity, and conflicts of interest among stakeholders, highlighting CVs as hybrid mechanisms that balance financial incentives and liquidity options.

title: Coherent Option Pricing
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University, SUNY at Binghamton - School of Management and Pennsylvania State University

detail.title: Coherent Option Pricing
