detail.abstract: The demand-based option pricing framework of Garleanu et al. (2009) assumes the existence of "end-users" of traded options who have an exogenous non-zero demand for option contracts, but is agnostic with respect to the nature of this demand. In this paper, we shed light on the demand for options by extending the binomial option pricing model to include risk-averse end-users with exogenous exposure to the underlying asset and imperfect delta-hedging by market makers. We derive analytical expressions for supply and demand curves in the index options market. Our model results closely mimic several empirical features of the index options market, including the persistence of a heterogeneous implied volatility surface and time-series correlations between the implied volatility skew and forward-looking measures of investor sentiment.

title: "Beyond the Language Barrier: Digital Divides and Environmental Participation in Immigrant Communities"

detail.title: "Beyond the Language Barrier: Digital Divides and Environmental Participation in Immigrant Communities"
detail.abstract: Municipal environmental communication strategies increasingly rely on digital platforms, yet these approaches may systematically exclude immigrant communities who face cultural, linguistic, and technological barriers to accessing environmental information. This study examines communication barriers among first-generation immigrants in the Greater Toronto Area through a cross-sectional survey of 815 participants across four age cohorts, measuring English proficiency, digital literacy, and municipal resource awareness.

detail.abstract: The failure of mine slopes constitutes one of the most serious dangers to surface mine and openpit mining operations as it causes serious harm to the safety of workers, continuation of the operations, and economic viability. Traditional monitoring methods like geotechnical sensors, embracing a periodic visual check and statistical prediction methods, tend to fail in delivering near-real-time, precise and flexible estimations. Such constraints create an acute demand on intelligent systems that will work with complex high-dimensional data in dynamic mining environments. The general approach of deep learning with its ability of automated feature selection and nonlinear pattern recognition provides a revolutionary method of slope stability monitoring. The Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), specifically, a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model, allow fusing various kinds of sensor data, including InSAR images, ground-based radar, accelerometers, and acoustic emissions. These models have the ability to ascertain spatial-temporal relationships, which can be used to forerun indicators of instabilities earlier than the traditional approaches. The present paper discusses the tool of deep learning models use in real-time monitoring and early warning systems of slope failures. It also emphasizes using sensor networks, big data platforms, predictive analytics in a comprehensive framework that would significantly increase the accuracy and timeliness of hazard detection. A specific focus is given to model adaptability, scalability, and pragmatic implementation both in mining and resource-limited production operations and those that have a high technology profile. This could save lives in the case of an attack because of the reduced probability of false alarms and hence the earlier interventions that could be sent and provide help on time. These consequences include better safety of the workers, fewer economic losses, and greater sustainability of the mining. This paper ends by outlining the research gaps such as explainable AI to support transparency, edge computing to support low latency analysis, and the need to establish some form of policy framework to standardize AI-driven geotechnical monitoring systems.

title: Dynamic Delegation with Reputation Feedback
affiliations: and Ecole Polytechnique

detail.title: Dynamic Delegation with Reputation Feedback
detail.abstract: We study dynamic delegation with reputation feedback: a long-lived expert advises a sequence of implementers whose effort responds to current reputation, altering outcome informativeness and belief updates. We solve for a recursive, belief-based equilibrium and show that advice is a reputation-dependent cutoff in the expert's signal. A diagnosticity condition-failures at least as informative as successes-implies reputational conservatism: the cutoff (weakly) rises with reputation. Comparative statics are transparent: greater private precision or a higher good-state prior lowers the cutoff, whereas patience (value curvature) raises it. Reputation is a submartingale under competent types and a supermartingale under less competent types; we separate boundary hitting into learning (news generated infinitely often) versus no-news absorption. A success-contingent bonus implements any target experimentation rate with a plug-in calibration in a Gaussian benchmark. The framework yields testable predictions and a measurement map for surgery (operate vs. conservative care).

detail.title: Beyond Words: Fed Chairs' Voice Sentiments and US Bank Stock Price Crash Risk

publicationDetails.detailsText: Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper No. 25-72

detail.abstract: Building on the methodology of Gorodnichenko et al. (2023), we reconstruct and propose a novel measure that quantifies the voice sentiment of the Chair of the Federal Reserve press conference responses and examine its impact on the stock price crash risk of U.S. banks. We find that a more positive vocal sentiment, indicative of happiness, significantly reduces banks' ex-ante crash risk, whereas negative emotions, such as sadness and anger, amplify it. Our findings suggest that, beyond the textual content of monetary policy statements, the emotional delivery of central bank communication plays a critical role in shaping financial stability outcomes.

title: What Works for Working Couples? Work Arrangements, Maternal Labor Supply, and the Division of Home Production
affiliations: University of Nottingham - School of Economics and New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: What Works for Working Couples? Work Arrangements, Maternal Labor Supply, and the Division of Home Production
detail.abstract: We provide the first causal evidence that changes to work arrangements – in the form of greater schedule regularity – can reduce the child penalty in earnings for women. The Australian 2009 Fair Work Act explicitly entitled parents of young children to request a change in work arrangements. Leveraging variation in the timing of the law, timing of childbirth, and the bite of the law across different occupations and industries, we establish three main results. First, new mothers used the Fair Work Act to maintain a regular schedule while reducing hours upon childbirth. Second, thanks to increased regularity, working mothers’ child penalty declined from a 47 to a 38 percent drop in hours worked. Third, while this increase in maternal labor supply implies a significant shift towards equality in the female- and male-shares of household income, we do not observe any changes in the female share of home production.

title: When Am I Richer than You? Toward a Meaningful Comparison of Income of Nations
affiliations: Concordia University, Quebec - Department of Economics and University of Bergen

detail.title: When Am I Richer than You? Toward a Meaningful Comparison of Income of Nations
detail.abstract: Per-capita national income remains a primary indicator of wellbeing in an international comparison. Accordingly, the World Bank has popularised the concept of constant-dollar income of a given base year (say 2015), which converts income denominated in constant local currency units (LCU) to a common base year and uses the market exchange rate of that year to derive the ‘2015 constant-USD’ income which is directly comparable across nations. The issue we address here centres on the evolving base year; with each change, a new constant USD income series is born embodying the base-year market exchange rate, which tends to be volatile. Predictably, the prior ranking of income of any two countries may well get reversed. To be concrete, as per 2010-base, Japan’s per capita GDP appeared to have peaked in 1991 at 10.4 percentage points above the US level, but by the constant 2015 metric, the 1991 Japanese income was only about 3/4th. Was Japan actually richer than the US in 1991? In an attempt to answer this, we propose replacing the market rate by a smoothed exchange rate. We then compare the smoothed exchange rates as well as the resulting constant-dollar income series with the PPP exchange rate and PPP income. We show that some of the smoothed rates yield exchange rates that are at least as stable as the PPP, measure the exchange rate movement at par with PPP, and the predicted income levels appear mutually consistent with the PPP income.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of prenatal exposure to air pollution on early childhood cognitive development and the potential mitigating role of nutritional interventions in China. Using variation in fetal exposure to PM2.5, we show that higher in-utero pollution levels reduce cognitive outcomes in early childhood. A randomized micronutrient supplementation program partially offsets these adverse effects, suggesting that improved nutrition can buffer some of the developmental damage caused by environmental shocks during gestation. These findings underscore the importance of complementary health and nutrition policies in alleviating the long-term consequences of environmental risk in developing countries.

title: A Study of the Impacts of GST on Selected Service Sector Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises in Gujarat
affiliations: Sardar Vallabhbhai Global University

detail.title: A Study of the Impacts of GST on Selected Service Sector Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises in Gujarat
detail.abstract: The study explores how Gujarat’s service sector MSME units are affected by GST. Direct and indirect taxes are the main sources of income for the Indian government; the latter has undergone substantial reform over time. An important turning point in India’s tax system was the implementation of the Goods and Services Tax (GST), which replaced a complex system of state and central levies with a single, cohesive framework. Beginning in 1986, the first efforts towards GST reform were followed by the submission of the Constitution Amendment Bill in 2011 and the recommendations of the Kelkar Task Force’s in 2000. The Constitution (122nd Amendment) Bill of 2014 was passed in spite of early opposition, opening the door for the implementation of GST on 1 July, 2017. Three parts make up the GST system, which is organised around the idea of “One Nation, One Tax”: The Central GST (CGST), State GST (SGST), and Integrated GST (IGST). Goods and services are subject to the tax, which is divided into four tax slabs: 5%, 12%, 18%, and 28%. Certain goods, such as those relating to gold and diamonds, are subject to lower taxes, while some necessities are exempted. For luxury and demerit goods, there is a compensating cess. The Union Finance Minister and members from each state and Union Territory make up the GST Council, which is crucial in determining tax rates, exemptions, and compliance procedures. Micro, Small, and Medium-Sized Enterprises (MSMEs) have benefited greatly from the new tax regime’s simplified compliance requirements, which include composition levy schemes, threshold exemptions, and quarterly GST return files. GST regulations must be followed by service sector MSMEs having a turnover of at least Rs. 20 lakhs (Rs. 10 lakhs for special category states). This paper examines the historical evolution of GST in India, its structural framework, and the economic impact on businesses, particularly MSMEs. By analysing the benefits and challenges associated with GST implementation, this study aims to provide insights into its role in promoting economic integration and simplifying tax compliance.

title: Dietary Exposure to Toxic Trace Elements Through Cooked Rice in High Rice Consuming Populations: A Comprehensive Risk Assessment in Sri Lanka
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Colombo - Department of Zoology and Environment Sciences, Sabaragamuwa University of Sri Lanka and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Dietary Exposure to Toxic Trace Elements Through Cooked Rice in High Rice Consuming Populations: A Comprehensive Risk Assessment in Sri Lanka
detail.abstract: Toxic Trace Element (TTE) contamination in rice poses a significant public health challenge, especially in populations with high rice consumption like Sri Lanka. This study evaluated the dietary exposure risk by measuring cadmium(Cd), arsenic(As), lead(Pb), and chromium(Cr) in widely consumed rice varieties in cooked form. Median(IQR) concentrations of Cd, As, Pb, and Cr in raw rice were 0.032(0.054), 0.049(0.028), 0.095(0.123) and 0.376(0.366)mg kg-1ww respectively. Red-rice showed higher Cd and As, whereas white-rice accumulated more Pb and Cr (p>0.05). No notable differences in TTE levels were found between Traditional, Improved or Imported rice varieties(p>0.05). Parboiled rice contained higher TTEs than non-parboiled rice(p<0.05). No samples exceeded JECFA-ML for Cd or As, with one exceeding the ML-Pb. However, 20% of samples surpassed the stricter 0.1 mgkg-1 Cd threshold used in several rice-consuming countries. Cooking reduced TTE levels significantly(p<0.001). Estimated daily intakes(EDIs) od Cd, As, Pb and Cr for a 61.4 kg Sri Lankan-adult were 0.271(±0.279), 0.297(±0.126), 0.643(±0.500), and 0.379(±0.333) mg day-1. The JECFA-PTMI-Cd was exceeded by 8.3% of samples, while 25% surpassed the EFSA-TDI-Cd. Potential carcinogenic risks were evident for Cd, As and Cr even at average consumption levels. Country-specific thresholds are recommended for ongoing monitoring to safeguard consumers with high rice intake.

title: The Virtues of Clarity: Robert Dorfman, from Mathematical Programming to Environmental Economics

detail.title: The Virtues of Clarity: Robert Dorfman, from Mathematical Programming to Environmental Economics
detail.abstract: This article explores the career of American economist Robert Dorfman (1916-2002), that can be divided into three distinct phases. During the first phase (1938-1958), he made contributions to mathematical programming and statistics. The clarity of his work was particularly emphasized by his colleagues, who believed it greatly helped disseminate mathematical programming among economists in the 1950s. In the second phase (1959-1972), he contributed to water management. His work during this phase was more applied and characterized by its interdisciplinary nature. Notably, he collaborated with oceanographers, political scientists, and sanitation engineers. Again, his explanations of the economic approach to water management and the relevance of mathematical programming in this context were praised for their clarity. During the third phase (1972-1997), he moved away from the specific case of water to focus more broadly on environmental economics, especially on critiques of cost-benefit analysis. By retracing his career, this article sheds light on the links among his various contributions and the role that clarity plays in how an economist's work is received.

title: Sniffing the Context: Divergent Effects of Odor Valence on Intertemporal Choice in Loss vs. Gain Frames
affiliations: Southwest Jiaotong University, Southwest Jiaotong University, Southwest Jiaotong University and Southwest Jiaotong University

detail.title: Sniffing the Context: Divergent Effects of Odor Valence on Intertemporal Choice in Loss vs. Gain Frames
detail.abstract: Olfactory cues, processed via direct limbic connections, can potently modulate affective states, yet their influence on complex decisions like intertemporal choice (involving trade-offs between immediate and delayed outcomes) have received scant attention in the research literature. Grounded in hyperbolic discounting models, this study used within-subjects experiment to systematically investigate the impact of olfactory emotional valence on temporal discounting behavior. Forty-four participants (18 males, 26 females) performed an intertemporal choice task under pleasant (sweet orange essential oil) and unpleasant (sodium valerate) odor conditions, alongside a neutral (diluted water) control. The major findings are as follows: (1) A significant main effect of odor valence on choice was observed (F(2,86)=5.967, p<0.01, η2=0.122), with participants showing a stronger preference for the smaller-sooner (SS) option when exposed to unpleasant odors. (2) A significant main effect of task type emerged (F(1,86)=190.324, p<0.001, η2=0.816): the proportion of immediate choices was significantly higher in loss contexts than in gain contexts. (3) A significant odor valence × task type interaction was found (F(2,86)=3.402, p<0.05). Simple effect analyses revealed that unpleasant odors significantly increased decision impulsivity (more SS choices) specifically in the gain task (p<0.01), but not in the loss task. (4) Linear mixed-effects modeling indicated that odor valence influenced decision speed: the pleasant odor prolonged reaction times (RT) in both gain and loss contexts (p<0.001). Furthermore, the sequence of odor presentation dynamically modulated the expression of impulsivity over trials. These results reveal a context-specific mechanism by which olfactory emotions influence intertemporal choice, providing a theoretical basis for environmental sensory modulation of decision-making.

title: The Future of Crypto Asset Regulation under WTO Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: Vanderbilt Journal of Transnational Law, forthcoming

detail.abstract: Crypto assets (sometimes referred to as cryptocurrencies) were created shortly after the 2008 financial crisis to provide an alternative financial system that was completely decentralized, trustless, and did not require any regulatory oversight. Since their inception, crypto assets have been plagued by violent value fluctuations and instances of severe negligence and fraud, causing billions of dollars in losses for investors every year. Despite the significant risks, the crypto asset economy has grown considerable over the past two decades, with more and more people around the world investing in crypto assets. The growth of the crypto asset economy, its increased interconnection with the traditional financial sector, and the lack of prudential safeguards in most countries, has prompted international financial institutions to increasingly voice their concerns regarding the risks to consumers and financial stability. Without a globally coordinated approach to the regulation of crypto assets, policy responses have diverged considerably. While the European Union recently enacted the Markets in Crypto Assets Regulation, imposing strict transparency, oversight and consumer protection requirements, the U.S. is trending towards "light touch" regulation of crypto assets under the second Trump administration.

title: Narcissism and Wellbeing in Midlife and Beyond

detail.title: Narcissism and Wellbeing in Midlife and Beyond
detail.abstract: Lauded psychotherapist and narcissism expert Otto Kernberg claimed that midlife crises were almost solely a narcissistic phenomenon. This article, in part, takes this claim as inspiration and investigates the relationship between grandiose narcissism and wellbeing. Importantly, and following previous research, this work considers grandiose narcissism in two distinct ways: an agentic admiration aspect (example statement: "Being a special person gives me strength") and an antagonistic rivalry aspect ("Most people are basically losers"). The results, obtained from an assessment of life satisfaction with a large nationally representative dataset, offer support to the previous small and largely homogenous sample investigations regarding wellbeing and narcissism. The agentic aspect of grandiose narcissism being positive for wellbeing and the antagonistic aspect negative. Additionally, the results show that the midlife low is substantially deeper (shallower) and longer (shorter) for those who exhibit the rivalry (admiration) aspect of grandiose narcissism. Of particular note and novelty is the evidence that suggests males who exhibit the rivalry trait in older age experience almost no recovery from the common midlife low. This is a result that aligns well with several discussed theories.

title: Strategic Interactions in Environmental Pollution Regulation: A Tripartite Evolutionary Game Model with Pollution Accident Risks
affiliations: Shandong Technology and Business University, Shandong Technology and Business University, Shandong Technology and Business University and Shandong Technology and Business University

detail.title: Strategic Interactions in Environmental Pollution Regulation: A Tripartite Evolutionary Game Model with Pollution Accident Risks
detail.abstract: Environmental safety is of paramount importance to public health, economic development, and social stability. Effectively addressing corporate pollution constitutes a critical component of environmental governance and is essential for achieving high-quality development. This study constructs an evolutionary game model involving polluting enterprises, government regulatory agencies, and the public, incorporating the probability of environmental pollution incidents. By employing evolutionary game theory, the strategic interactions and dynamic evolution among the three stakeholders are systematically analyzed. Numerical simulations and sensitivity analyses are conducted to validate the theoretical findings. The results indicate that the strategic choices of polluting enterprises are jointly influenced by the probability of pollution incidents and the intensity of government regulation. When the incident probability is below a certain threshold, enterprises prefer legal discharge under strict regulation and illegal discharge under lax oversight; above this threshold, legal discharge becomes the dominant strategy regardless of regulatory stringency. The model identifies two evolutionary stable strategies, one of which achieves Pareto optimality by aligning individual and collective interests. Moreover, the effectiveness of punitive measures outweighs that of rewards in promoting compliance, and sanctions from higher-level governments significantly enhance local regulatory responsiveness. Key parameters—such as pollution and regulatory costs, pollution probability, and public loss—exert varying degrees of influence on strategic evolution. The study provides theoretical implications for the mitigation of corporate pollution and the enhancement of environmental risk governance.

title: The Transmission of Reliable and Unreliable Information
affiliations: Harvard Business School, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and University of Cologne

detail.title: The Transmission of Reliable and Unreliable Information
detail.abstract: Information often shapes behavior regardless of its quality: unreliable claims wield influence, while reliable ones are neglected. We propose that this occurs in part because word-of-mouth transmission tends to preserve claims while dropping information about their reliability. We conduct controlled online experiments where participants listen to economic forecasts and pass them on through voice messages. Other participants listen either to original or transmitted audio recordings and report incentivized beliefs. Across various transmitter incentive schemes, a claim’s reliability is lost in transmission much more than the claim itself. Reliable and unreliable information, once filtered through transmission, impact listener beliefs similarly. Mechanism experiments show that reliability is lost not because it is perceived as less relevant or harder to transmit, but because it is less likely to come to mind during transmission. A simple associative-memory framework suggests that reliability information may be less likely to come to mind either because it is less likely to be cued by transmission requests or because attempts to retrieve it face greater interference. Evidence from our experiments, a large corpus of everyday conversations, and economic TV news supports both of these mechanisms.

title: Income Effects and Optimal Taxation
affiliations: University of Oslo and

detail.title: Income Effects and Optimal Taxation
detail.abstract:
Recent empirical evidence points towards the importance of income effects for explaining labor supply decisions. While it has long been recognized that income effects matter for optimal taxation, their precise implications remain unclear. We show that income effects influence optimal tax rates through two distinct channels: the behavioral response channel, which captures how income effects alter workers' responsiveness to tax changes, and the government funds channel, which captures how income effects influence the value of tax revenue. While the behavioral response channel is well understood, the government funds channel has received less attention. We demonstrate that previous work has obtained optimal top tax rates that significantly exceed the true optimum by omitting the government funds channel.

Taking both channels into account, we derive results on how income effects shape optimal top-income tax rates and find that for a fixed uncompensated elasticity, income effects lower optimal tax rates. When the compensated elasticity is held fixed, the effect is ambiguous. We end by showing how our results generalize to settings where the whole tax system, not only the top income tax rate, is set optimally.

title: The National Carbon Price and Welfare on Alternative Paths Towards Net Zero Emissions: Simple Versus Optimal Policy Rules
affiliations: University of Copenhagen and University of Copenhagen - Department of Economics

detail.title: The National Carbon Price and Welfare on Alternative Paths Towards Net Zero Emissions: Simple Versus Optimal Policy Rules

keywords: Hotelling Rule for optimal climate policy

detail.abstract: To study the economic and welfare consequences of alternative time paths towards net zero CO2e emissions, we develop a multi-sector dynamic computable general equilibrium model of an open economy with heterogeneity in abatement costs across sectors and firms and with adjustment costs in the adoption of abatement technologies and other types of investment. We measure the welfare costs of following the simple rules for emissions reduction observed in practice rather than the optimal national policy rule prescribed by economic theory. In an undistorted economy subject to a carbon budget, the theoretically optimal climate policy is a "Hotelling rule" where the carbon tax rate increases year by year at the real rate of interest. However, when some consumers are credit-constrained, it is optimal to deviate from the Hotelling rule and use carbon taxation to redistribute income towards poor hand-to-mouth consumers. Nevertheless, in aggregate terms very little welfare is lost by following a Hotelling rule or a linear emissions reduction path rather than the optimal time path for carbon taxes when climate policy is subject to a carbon budget. The optimal carbon tax path towards a simple end-point target for net zero emissions implies a much higher welfare cost per ton of accumulated GHG emissions than a policy constrained by a carbon budget.

title: Intergenerational Population Ethics
affiliations: University of St. Gallen

detail.title: Intergenerational Population Ethics
detail.abstract: This paper characterizes a novel class of welfare criteria for settings with endogenous population. The core innovation is to treat parents’ fertility preferences as ethically relevant, deferring to them on the quality–quantity trade-off under conditions of equality. The resulting family of criteria generalizes discounted utilitarianism by reconciling respect for parents’ fertility preferences with equity across generations. These criteria resolve long-standing normative dilemmas that afflict existing approaches to population ethics, such as total and average utilitarianism. After formal characterization, I illustrate the criterion in stylized examples and a Barro–Becker environment.

title: Risk Assessment of Driver Emotion Using a Data-Driven Bayesian Network: Insights from a Naturalistic Driving Study
affiliations: Virginia Tech, Virginia Tech Transportation Institute, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Virginia Tech Transportation Institute, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Virginia Tech

detail.title: Risk Assessment of Driver Emotion Using a Data-Driven Bayesian Network: Insights from a Naturalistic Driving Study
detail.abstract: Driving in a state of high emotions, particularly anger, can impair driving abilities and increase the risk of crashes. Understanding the influencing factors on emotions and how emotions impact safety-critical events (SCEs) is crucial for enhancing traffic safety. This study aims to investigate the relationship between emotions and SCEs on the road, considering various contributing factors such as driver demographics, traffic conditions, and road geography. Through a data-driven Bayesian Network (BN), we validate the relationships among these factors and assess their joint impact on SCEs. By employing domain expert knowledge and a hybrid structure learning approach, we construct an BN structure that effectively captures the dependencies among different variables. Clear dependency relationships are identified, with traffic flow directly influencing emotion and factors like traffic density, secondary tasks, emotion, and driving errors significantly affecting SCEs. Through BN inference, we explore the marginal and joint effects of various factors on SCEs, highlighting the increased SCE risk associated with emotions, driving errors, high traffic density, and secondary tasks. The identification of high-risk scenarios provides valuable insights for targeted intervention and mitigation efforts. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of the relationship between emotions and SCEs, offering methods for enhancing road safety measures and accident prevention strategies.

title: How Do Caseworkers Affect Job Search Outcomes?
affiliations: University of Vienna

detail.title: How Do Caseworkers Affect Job Search Outcomes?
detail.abstract: This paper examines how caseworkers influence job finding rates and job quality. To rule out selection effects, I exploit that caseworkers are assigned based on the jobseekers’ month of birth in some offices of the Austrian public employment service. Combining administrative data on caseworkers and jobseekers, I compute value-added measures for multiple jobseeker outcomes. A one-standard-deviation increase in caseworker performance corresponds to six additional days of employment in the first year and two percent higher earnings. For older workers and workers of foreign nationality, I observe the largest differences in caseworker performance. Employment and earnings effects are positively correlated, suggesting that faster job finding does not come at the expense of job quality. Analyzing differences in caseworker strategies, I find that caseworkers who refer more vacancies to jobseekers achieve higher employment rates, and those who refer better-paying jobs also achieve higher earnings. In contrast, frequent use of training programs or benefit sanctions is associated with worse job search outcomes.

title: Monetary Policy Shocks and Firms' Investment Decisions
affiliations: ETH Zürich - KOF Swiss Economic Institute, ETH Zurich, ETH Zurich and ETH Zürich - KOF Swiss Economic Institute

detail.title: Monetary Policy Shocks and Firms' Investment Decisions
detail.abstract: We study the investment channel of monetary policy through a randomized survey experiment, exposing Swiss firms directly to shocks to the Swiss National Bank’s policy rate. Our survey experiment randomizes pure policy-rate shocks—uncontaminated by information effects—and records firms’ revisions to investment plans and financing choices. We find pronounced asymmetry: firms respond strongly to unanticipated rate hikes but only moderately to equivalent cuts. This asymmetry varies with firm size, sector, export intensity, and investment types. Investment financing shapes the response: reliance on internal funds and being financially unconstrained amplifies investment sensitivity.

title: Unfair Chances and Labor Supply
affiliations: Aarhus University, Department of Economics and Business Economics, Maastricht University and Maastricht University

detail.title: Unfair Chances and Labor Supply
detail.abstract: We conduct an online experiment to study how the unfairness of chances leading to wage inequality affects labor supply decisions. We find that, at a given wage, disadvantageous wage inequality reduces labor supply, but whether this inequality stems from fair or unfair chances does not matter. That is, a procedure with fair chances does not compensate for wage inequality. Our results stand in stark contrast to prior empirical evidence showing that individuals care about fair chances when making equity judgments.

title: Direct Air Capture and interactions with the electricity market
affiliations: Norwegian University of Life Sciences and Norwegian University of Life Sciences

detail.title: Direct Air Capture and interactions with the electricity market
detail.abstract: Direct Air Capture (DAC) might become an important technology in the future, due to a need of negative CO2 emissions. DAC operation is very energy intensive, and large-scale use of DAC will thus impact the electricity market. Meanwhile, electricity generation is becoming more volatile with bigger share of intermittent technologies. This paper examines possible interactions between the electricity market and adoption of DAC technologies. Combining theoretical analysis with stylized numerical simulations, we show that DAC adoption can increase or decrease electricity price volatility, depending on the choice of DAC technology. Cost reductions or improved energy efficiency for the most energy-efficient technology tends to increase price volatility, as it reduces the deployment of the more energy-intensive DAC technology, which is more likely to be turned off when prices are high. Further, higher CO2 prices increase the deployment of the most energy-efficient technology to a larger degree than the more energy-intensive one.

title: When Disaster Strikes: How Climate Events Influence Employment Preferences
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology - Department of Accounting, , Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Accounting and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School

detail.title: When Disaster Strikes: How Climate Events Influence Employment Preferences
detail.abstract: This paper examines how experiences with climate disasters shape workers’ employment preferences. We find that, in disaster-affected areas, firms with worse environmental performance fill vacancies more slowly and hire lower quality employees than better environmentally performing firms, compared to unaffected areas. The job vacancy effect strengthens where belief in climate change is greater. After disasters, local employees at environmentally worse-performing firms leave more negative employer reviews about environmental issues and are more likely to move to greener employers, relative to other-location employees. Overall, our evidence suggests that climate disasters increase workers’ climate awareness and their preference for environmentally responsible employers.

title: The Dual Strategy of Exclusion and Engagement: Impact on Asset Prices and Green Transition
affiliations: and University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne)

detail.title: The Dual Strategy of Exclusion and Engagement: Impact on Asset Prices and Green Transition

publicationDetails.detailsText: Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper No. 25-74
publicationDetails.journalName: Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical asset-pricing model to examine how sustainable investors can combine exclusion and engagement strategies to accelerate corporate transition. Firms are classified as green, brown, or reformable, with the latter being polluting firms that can reduce emissions under shareholder pressure. Sustainable investors exclude brown firms but may engage with reformable ones when majority ownership enables them to enforce a transition. Engagement is modeled as a costly but effective mechanism that lowers emissions and generates non-pecuniary benefits for investors. Our main result is that only a moderate share of sustainable investors (around 22.5% of market wealth) is sufficient to trigger reformable firms' transition, provided they derive a modest non-pecuniary benefit (about 2.3%) from sustainability improvements. In this equilibrium, sustainable investors are willing to concentrate their portfolios in reformable assets, enabling these firms to adopt cleaner technologies and reduce their environmental footprint. The model shows that a relatively small but motivated coalition of investors can induce meaningful environmental change through targeted engagement.

title: In the Mood to Exclude: A Defense of Digital Property Rights Against GenAI Scraping
affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin, TX, USA

detail.title: In the Mood to Exclude: A Defense of Digital Property Rights Against GenAI Scraping
detail.abstract:
This paper argues that website owners have the right to exclude others from their websites. Accordingly, when generative AI (GenAI) scraping bots intentionally circumvent reasonable technological barriers, their conduct should be actionable as trespass to chattels. The prevailing judicial focus on website content and the dismissal of trespass claims absent proof of server impairment or user disruption misconstrues the nature of the website itself as a form of digital property and focuses too narrowly on what constitutes harm under a claim of trespass. By shifting analysis from content to the website itself as an integrated digital asset and illustrating the harm to the value of the chattel, this paper demonstrates that the right to exclude applies online with the same force as it does to tangible property. 

This doctrinal reframing has urgent significance in the GenAI era. Courts and litigants have struggled to police large-scale scraping because copyright preemption narrows available claims, leaving copyright and its fair use defense as the primary battleground. In contrast, recognizing websites as personal property revives trespass to chattels as a meaningful cause of action, providing website owners with an enforceable exclusionary right. Such protection would disincentivize exploitative scraping, preserve incentives for content creation, aid in protecting privacy and personal data, and safeguard values of autonomy and expression. Ultimately, this paper contends that reaffirming website owners' right to exclude is essential to maintaining a fair and sustainable online environment.

title: Towards a Blunder-Free Society: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Optimizing Collective Outcomes through Blunder Avoidance and Cooperative Strategies

detail.title: Towards a Blunder-Free Society: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Optimizing Collective Outcomes through Blunder Avoidance and Cooperative Strategies
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for conceptualizing the "best society" as one where complex thinking entities avoid blunders-knowingly suboptimal actionsthereby optimizing the impact of human actions on individual and collective life curves. Drawing from game theory, behavioral economics, and psychological metaphors, we redefine luck primarily as the externalities of others' blunders, with rare random hazards as negligible factors. Using the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD) as a core model, we demonstrate through simulations that strategies like tit-for-tat foster cooperation and maximize outcomes, proving that universal blunder avoidance leads to systemic trust and prosperity. New additions include the five factors of good outcomes, ethics as uncertainty of value, and net value calculation for retrospective action judgment. Educational implications are discussed, advocating for curricula that teach blunder recognition and best ethics to realize this ideal. Simulations confirm that blunder-free environments yield outcomes approaching optimal values (e.g., normalized O ≈ 0.6), supporting our hypothesis. [? ? ? ]

title: Questions, Measures, and Meaning: Interpreting Indicators from the ifo Business Survey
affiliations: Ifo Institute, Ifo Institute and Ifo Institute

detail.title: Questions, Measures, and Meaning: Interpreting Indicators from the ifo Business Survey
detail.abstract: In addition to the well-known ifo Business Climate Index for Germany, the ifo Business Survey generates a wide range of further indicators based on monthly responses from around 9,000 companies across all major sectors. These indicators capture current business conditions, expectations, constraints, and sector-specific developments, and many have proven to be valuable leading signals for macroeconomic analysis. This paper provides a systematic guide to interpreting these indicators. We explain the main types of survey questions, outline the methods used to transform responses into economically meaningful measures, and highlight key aspects to consider when interpreting results. Practical examples illustrate how the indicators can be applied in economic analysis, policy advice, and business decision-making.

title: Do Investors Care about Sustainable Investment Targets? An Assessment Using the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation
affiliations: Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE and

detail.title: Do Investors Care about Sustainable Investment Targets? An Assessment Using the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation

declarations.funderStatement: We gratefully acknowledge research support from the Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE.

publicationDetails.journalName: Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the impact of disclosures of sustainable investment targets under the EU Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) on mutual fund flows. Using a staggered difference-indifferences setup and focusing on retail-oriented index funds, we find that sustainable investment targets have a temporarily positive impact on fund flows in comparison to funds without sustainable investment targets. Furthermore, we find a negative linear relationship between sustainable investment targets and fund flows. While lower targets attract higher fund inflows, higher targets result in significantly lower or even no inflows. Our results suggest that up to a target level of 20% in sustainable investments, index funds can attract more inflows. This suggests a trade-off between sustainability commitments and performance considerations.

title: Can Firms Gain from Wage Transparency Mandates in the Presence of Minimum Wage Requirements?
affiliations: Fudan University - School of Management, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management and Shanghai University - School of Management

detail.title: Can Firms Gain from Wage Transparency Mandates in the Presence of Minimum Wage Requirements?
detail.abstract: Problem Definition: We develop a stylized model to examine wage transparency in the presence of minimum wage laws. While transparency can foster consumer trust and attract socially conscious buyers, it also exposes firms to scrutiny over pricing fairness-especially in states enforcing both wage transparency laws and binding minimum wages. These overlapping mandates raise concerns about rising prices, shrinking profits, and potential job losses. Despite growing attention, formal economic analysis of these dynamics remains limited. Methodology/Results: We present a stylized model to analyze wage transparency under minimum wage laws, examining firms' incentives to exceed wage floors, the effects on pricing and profits, and when transparency is advantageous. We compare equilibrium outcomes under opaque vs. transparent policies in monopoly and duopoly markets, accounting for consumer sensitivity to price, transparency, and fairness. In monopolistic markets, wage transparency mandates lead firms to offer higher wages and expand hiring. When consumers show limited concern for profit margin fairness, transparency allows firms to raise prices and improve profits. In duopolistic markets, these benefits largely persist. However, if consumers prioritize fairness in profit margins over wage transparency, competitive pressures may suppress wages and reduce employment. When fairness concerns are moderate, transparency enhances outcomes for both firms and workers, especially when paired with elevated wage floors. In "asymmetric market-size" duopolies, smaller firms gain more from transparency than larger rivals. In "asymmetric labor preference" duopolies, wage transparency mandates favor less preferred firms at low wage floors but benefit preferred firms more at moderate levels. At high wage floors, both firms benefit. Managerial Implications: These findings challenge the notion that wage transparency in the presence of minimum wage requirements undermines firm performance and labor market health.

title: The Rise of Work from Home and its Impact on Job Satisfaction
affiliations: University of Southern California, University of Southern California - Center for Economic and Social Research (CESR) and University of Southern California - Center for Economic and Social Research (CESR)

detail.title: The Rise of Work from Home and its Impact on Job Satisfaction

keywords.keywords: Job satisfactionWork From HomeNon monetary aspects of workremote work

detail.abstract: The pandemic induced dramatic changes in work arrangements, particularly through a steep increase in Work from Home (WFH) prevalence. Starting in 2021, we fielded yearly surveys about WFH in a nationally representative, probability-based-sampled panel. We use discrete choice experiments to elicit the valuation that workers assign to the possibility of working from home. We then study how the possibility of working from home affects workers’ job satisfaction. Workers who can WFH are more satisfied with their jobs compared to those who cannot. Fixed-effects models confirm that workers report higher job satisfaction when their preferences for WFH are accommodated by their employers. Using panel data covering both the period before and during the COVID-19 pandemic, we then show that workers who had WFH-amenable jobs at the time of the pandemic’s onset experienced an increase in satisfaction with job and daily activities compared to those with jobs not amenable to WFH. This relative increase persists years after the pandemic’s onset, and remains significant in 2024. Since the increased availability of WFH opportunities mainly benefited individuals of higher socioeconomic status, the pandemic-induced transformation of work arrangements has widened inequalities in job satisfaction. Our calculations suggest that, once the regressive nature of the shift toward remote work is taken into account, the resulting changes in utility approximately offset the relative earnings gains observed among lower-income workers between 2019 and 2023.

title: Geometric Necessity: Resolving the Ellipse Perimeter Problem with Discrete Lattice Computation
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Geometric Necessity: Resolving the Ellipse Perimeter Problem with Discrete Lattice Computation
detail.abstract: The ellipse perimeter problem, unsolved for over 300 years due to the absence of an elementary closed-form expression, is resolved through a novel discrete computational method rooted in the Tetrahedral-Octahedral (TH-OH) lattice geometry. This paper presents a Python implementation that computes the perimeter of an ellipse (A=1.5, B=1.0) as 7.944032 units using a constructible constant , outperforming traditional approximations like Ramanujan's 7.932 units. By rejecting unconstructible transcendental constants (e.g.,) and infinite series, this approach demonstrates that discrete, finite geometry supersedes continuous models, shattering the foundation of classical computational geometry.

title: ADHD Symptom Magnitude Predicts Creative Problem-Solving Performance and Insight Versus Analysis Solving Modes
affiliations: Drexel University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Drexel University, Drexel University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Drexel University

detail.title: ADHD Symptom Magnitude Predicts Creative Problem-Solving Performance and Insight Versus Analysis Solving Modes
detail.abstract: Although Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is linked to executive-function deficits, research suggests that it may benefit creativity. We hypothesized that ADHD symptom severity is associated with distinct problem-solving modes. In this online study, 301 participants solved Compound Remote Associates problems to assess whether ADHD symptoms, measured by the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale, predict insight-based (“Aha!”) versus analytic problem-solving. Individuals with the highest ADHD symptom severity relied more on insight than analysis compared to those with the lowest symptoms. Both the high- and low-ADHD symptom groups outperformed those in the middle of the distribution, suggesting that strong and weak executive function facilitate different pathways to solution while moderate function benefits neither. Regression analyses showed that increasing ADHD symptoms decreased analytic solving but increased insight solving, resulting in an overall U-shaped function. These findings highlight two routes to creative problem solving: deliberate analysis versus spontaneous insight, the latter associated with stronger ADHD symptoms.

title: The Theology of Innovation: Unveiling the Divine Spark in Human Creativity
affiliations: African Research Network (ARN)

detail.title: The Theology of Innovation: Unveiling the Divine Spark in Human Creativity
detail.abstract: This article presents a comprehensive exploration of the emerging field of the "theology of innovation," which seeks to reframe the understanding of human creativity and technological progress within a theological and spiritual framework. Drawing from diverse sources, including biblical hermeneutics, the spirituality of innovation, the ethics of innovation, and the inspiration of spiritual intelligence, the article unveils the divine spark that animates the innovative impulse. Engaging in dialogue with contemporary thinkers from various disciplines, as well as the groundbreaking work of Congolese scholar Pitshou Moleka and his transdisciplinary science of "innovationology," this article offers a transformative vision for innovation that celebrates its sacred nature and its role in the ongoing work of the divine Creator. By embracing a holistic, spiritually-informed approach to innovation, this paradigm shift empowers us to navigate the complexities of the modern world with a renewed sense of purpose, responsibility, and reverence for the creative potential embedded within the human condition.

title: Strategic Regulatory Innovation: Mechanisms For Enhancing Corporate Financial Governance in the United States
affiliations: University of Illinois

detail.title: Strategic Regulatory Innovation: Mechanisms For Enhancing Corporate Financial Governance in the United States
detail.abstract: This article discusses the importance of developing strategic new rules and regulations to enhance corporate financial governance in the United States.  Regulatory failures have been ongoing for a long time, as evident in the 2008 financial crisis and the FTX scandal. Traditional compliance-based models have been unable to address systemic risks and market complexity.  The paper advocates for a cohesive methodology that synchronizes legal frameworks with strategic foresight instruments, encompassing risk-based planning, stakeholder accountability, and performance metrics.  It examines the flaws in the Dodd-Frank Act, proposes changes based on corporate, trade, and commercial law, and draws on examples from the U.S. and Greece to illustrate the consequences of inadequate regulatory strategies.  It also examines how strategic management tools can facilitate proactive enforcement and enhance institutional strength.  The article examines national benefits, including improved investor confidence, reduced regulatory friction, and goals aligned with inclusive economic development.  The paper concludes by urging policymakers, regulators, and financial institutions to adopt a proactive regulatory framework that integrates compliance into their business strategies.   The paper argues that the U.S. can enhance its financial stability, foster greater openness, and establish itself as a world leader in flexible and sustainable financial governance by adopting this approach.

title: Adaptive Self-Perception Hypothesis: An Evolutionary Model of Self-Recognition Strategies
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Adaptive Self-Perception Hypothesis: An Evolutionary Model of Self-Recognition Strategies
detail.abstract: Distortions of self-perception—such as overconfidence in the less skilled and impostor feelings in the highly skilled—are often treated as cognitive errors. The Adaptive Self-Perception Hypothesis reframes these patterns as distinct adaptive strategies shaped by evolutionary and social pressures. Individuals can be classified into three types: Ordinary, relying on overconfidence and self-promotion to secure short-term advantages; Talented, emphasizing effort, reproducibility, and adherence to norms to build mid-term trust and stability; and Exceptional, adopting humility or impostor tendencies to sustain long-term creativity and avoid suppression.  This framework integrates fragmented constructs including the Dunning–Kruger effect, growth mindset, and impostor phenomenon into a unified model of individual differences. It predicts systematic divergence between actual and perceived ability across the three types: Ordinary individuals tend to be overestimated, Talented individuals remain aligned, and Exceptional individuals are underestimated. The model further explains mutual recognition patterns, interpersonal dynamics, and organizational biases that favor perceived ability over actual competence. Mapping onto Big Five and HEXACO dimensions provides conceptual grounding, while cultural psychology clarifies differences in prevalence across societies. Implications extend to education, organizational design, and cross-cultural innovation.

title: The Jurisprudence of Syntax and the Institution of Meaning
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: The Jurisprudence of Syntax and the Institution of Meaning
detail.abstract: Language mirrors the human ecosystem with startling fidelity. Its layers align with the architecture of governance: grammar resembles state structure, syntax corresponds to jurisprudence, semantics embodies institutions, and pragmatics echoes society in practice. This essay unfolds that analogy while also challenging its limits. Using insights from Douglass North on institutions, from complexity science on emergence, and from philosophy of language on meaning, it argues that language is not merely reflective but also constitutive of human order. The jurisprudence of syntax and the institution of meaning do not just describe society; they shape its frozen accidents and emergent trajectories.

title: From the Madness of More to the Wisdom of Enough: Ecogovernance as a Solution to Capitalism's Terminal Crisis

detail.title: From the Madness of More to the Wisdom of Enough: Ecogovernance as a Solution to Capitalism's Terminal Crisis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interests.

detail.abstract: We're facing what might be capitalism's terminal crisis-ecological collapse, economic stagnation, and social fragmentation converging in ways that suggest fundamental system breakdown. Fifty years after The Limits to Growth warned about planetary boundaries, we seem trapped in what I call the "madness of more"-a compulsive cycle of endless expansion that undermines the very foundations it depends on. While recognising it is not a panacea, this paper explores ecogovernance through natural legal personhood as one potential systemic response. The concept is straightforward: what if natural entities could become economic agents? Rivers owning companies, forests directing investments, ecosystems participating in strategic decisions. Drawing on empirical evidence and legal precedents from rights of nature initiatives globally, along with theoretical frameworks from Moore's world ecology, Holling's panarchy, and Ostrom's commons research, I examine how granting economic agency to natural entities might break the structural compulsions driving ecological destruction. Most importantly, this approach could address something most technological and policy solutions miss: the cultural and psychological dimensions of our ecological crisis. When we recognise natural entities as subjects deserving representation rather than objects for extraction, we might catalyse the worldview shift that genuine sustainability requires.

title: Autonomy and Metapreferences
affiliations: Université Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne - Centre d'Economie de la Sorbonne (CES)

detail.title: Autonomy and Metapreferences
detail.abstract: To adequately describe notions like "autonomy" or "responsibility" within the standard economic model of rational choice, it is necessary to introduce metapreferences ---that is, preferences over preferences. This paper develops two models of metapreferences: a "hierarchical" model, involving second-order preferences, third-order preferences, etc., and a "recursive" model, involving a type space where each type determines preferences over type-outcome pairs. For each model, the paper introduces concepts of internal coherence and rational choice. It then studies the relationship between the two models.

title: Cost-effectiveness Of Screening and Treatment Protocols for Treating Hepatic Encephalopathy in Patients Diagnosed with Dementia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) - School of Pharmacy, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU)

detail.title: Cost-effectiveness Of Screening and Treatment Protocols for Treating Hepatic Encephalopathy in Patients Diagnosed with Dementia
detail.abstract: BackgroundA portion of patients diagnosed as dementia could instead have cirrhosis and reversible hepatic encephalopathy (HE). Strategies to identify and treat reversible HE in patients currently diagnosed as dementia could prevent misdiagnosis and unnecessary healthcare resource use.ObjectiveDetermine cost-effectiveness of easily available strategies (Fibrosis-4 FIB-4) score, HE treatments (lactulose/rifaximin) and hepatology involvement for HE diagnosis in dementia patients.MethodsThis study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of screening and treatment strategies for HE in patients with dementia, using a decision-analytic model from a societal perspective. A decision tree model compared seven strategies over a 1-year time horizon. Six strategies (FIB-4+empiric lactulose, FIB-4+empiric rifaximin, FIB-4+hepatology input+lactulose, FIB-4+hepatology input+rifaximin, Empiric lactulose for all, empiric rifaximin for all) were compared to status quo.ResultsFive of six intervention strategies showed higher effectiveness at lower cost versus status quo, with savings ranging from $6,160 to $13,236. The most economically efficient strategy was FIB-4 screening followed by hepatology consultation and targeted lactulose therapy, which generated cost savings and a gain in outcomes compared with no screening. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness of screening strategies, with results most influenced by treatment response, utility values, and cirrhosis prevalence.ConclusionsThe combination of FIB-4 screening, hepatology referral, and lactulose therapy offers the best balance of value and clinical benefit, avoiding unnecessary overtreatment while capturing reversible cases of HE. Targeted HE screening in patients with dementia is cost-effective, improves diagnostic accuracy, reduces healthcare costs, and offers an opportunity to reverse cognitive impairment in individuals otherwise presumed to have irreversible dementia.

title: Beyond the Click: The New Currencies of the AI Search Era

detail.title: Beyond the Click: The New Currencies of the AI Search Era
detail.abstract:
Google’s Generalised Second-Price (GSP) auction has long underpinned the $200 billion click-based search economy. However, the rise of AI-driven search – through Google AI Overviews, AI Mode, and agentic systems – undermines GSP’s central assumption that clicks are a reliable proxy for advertiser value. AI systems increasingly fulfil user intent within the interface, producing the 'Great Decoupling' of impressions and clicks. 

This paper analyses how these shifts erode the incentive structure of GSP and misprice informational influence, particularly in high-trust 'Your Money or Your Life' domains. Drawing on mechanism design, it proposes a novel two-stage auction – the Authority and Action framework – that prices both upstream informational authority and downstream transactional fulfilment. The model incorporates an Authority Gate, Trust Tokens, and hierarchical topic targeting to align incentives across multi-session user journeys. 

By reconceptualising trust and semantic authority as economic assets, this framework restores efficiency in AI-mediated markets while preserving user trust. The findings carry strategic implications for digital advertising and open a broader research agenda on pricing mechanisms in machine-mediated economies.

title: Do Investor Sentiments Affect the Link between Agricultural and Energy Commodity Markets?
affiliations: Louisiana State University - Department of Agricultural Economics & Agribusiness and University of Georgia

detail.title: Do Investor Sentiments Affect the Link between Agricultural and Energy Commodity Markets?
detail.abstract: This study investigates whether investor sentiments impact the dynamic relationship between agricultural and energy commodity markets. While existing research has extensively focused on structural linkages between these markets, such as through input costs, biofuel demand, and policy interventions, the role of behavioral factors remains underexplored. Using daily and weekly data on two commodity groups (corn-ethanol-crude oil and soybeans-soybean oil-biodiesel), we examine whether commodity-specific investor sentiments affect return correlations and shock transmission across markets. Sentiment is measured using the Thomson Reuters MarketPsych Index, which aggregates news- and media-based indicators. We employ a two-step empirical strategy: a Dynamic Conditional Correlation GARCH model to estimate time-varying return correlations, and a Time-Varying Parameter Vector Autoregression model to assess connectedness and spillovers. Our findings suggest that investor sentiments have a statistically significant and asymmetrical impact on market linkages. Negative sentiment in energy markets tends to weaken the correlation and connectedness with agricultural commodities, while positive sentiment has a more muted effect. Sentiment in agricultural markets, particularly corn and soybeans, also influences the linkages, but to a lesser extent. The results have important implications for risk management and policy. For market participants, ignoring sentiment can lead to miscalculating hedging effectiveness, while for policymakers, understanding sentiment-driven dynamics is critical for designing measures that stabilize agricultural and energy markets.

title: Deal Sourcing and Operational Risk Management
affiliations: University of Georgia - Terry College of Business, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and

detail.title: Deal Sourcing and Operational Risk Management
detail.abstract: Liquidity management is one of the most important responsibilities of CFOs and other accounting executives. Yet little is known about how the different tools for managing liquidity interact. We develop a dynamic model in which a firm engages in deal sourcingcostly effort to secure favorable opportunities for asset sales or acquisitions-and operational policies that stabilize cash flows at the expense of expected productivity. A liquidity constraint requiring nonnegative cash balances endogenously ties these policies together and gives rise to distinctive patterns. In particular, we find that the effort to manage the risk of operations declines monotonically with liquidity, while deal sourcing follows a U-shaped profile: intensive when liquidity is scarce (to support sales) or abundant (to pursue acquisitions), but limited at intermediate levels. Consequently, the two policies act as complements in low-liquidity states but substitutes in high-liquidity states. The framework maps directly into accounting statements, predicting systematic differences in firms' cash buffers, operating volatility, asset turnover, and payouts. These predictions speak to observed heterogeneity across industries with illiquid assets and provide guidance for empirical research.

title: Decentralized Autonomous Not-for-Profit Organization: Mechanism and Social Experiment
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Boston - College of Management

detail.title: Decentralized Autonomous Not-for-Profit Organization: Mechanism and Social Experiment
detail.abstract: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) have emerged as pioneering governance structures that enable collective decision-making without centralized authority. Yet their reliance on tokenweighted voting and financialized incentives often privileges wealth concentration, constrains participation, and narrows organizational success to market metrics. This paper introduces the concept of Decentralized Autonomous Non-Profit Organizations (DANPOs) as an innovative model designed to address these limitations. DANPOs reorient organizational value away from capital accumulation toward the cultivation of trust, belonging, and diversity of perspectives. Drawing on insights from organizational science, sociology, and blockchain studies, we examine how DANPOs can enhance community resilience through shared responsibility, sustained dialogue, and inclusive participation. We argue that DANPOs represent a critical evolution of decentralized governance, demonstrating how technology-mediated organizations can prioritize human connection and collective purpose over financial returns. The analysis contributes to ongoing debates on the future of organizing in digital societies.

title: The Impact of New York's 2025 Congestion Pricing on Traffic Volume
affiliations: San Francisco State University and

detail.title: The Impact of New York's 2025 Congestion Pricing on Traffic Volume
detail.abstract: This study evaluates the short-term impacts of New York City’s congestion pricing policy, introduced on January 5, 2025, on traffic volumes at key entry points into Manhattan. Using high-frequency traffic count data from the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (2010–2025), we focus on the Queens Midtown Tunnel (QMT), which is fully subject to the new toll, and compare it to partially and unaffected facilities—the Hugh L. Carey Tunnel (HCT) and Robert F. Kennedy Bridge (TBX). Employing a difference-in-differences design with 4AM traffic as the control, we find that congestion pricing led to a statistically significant reduction of approximately 135 vehicles per hour at QMT during charged hours. Robustness checks, including placebo tests and alternative model specifications, support these results. Spillover analysis reveals significant reductions at HCT but no evidence of diversion to TBX, suggesting the policy reduced overall driving demand rather than shifting routes. Our findings provide early empirical evidence that congestion pricing in New York achieved its goal of reducing vehicle volumes into the Central Business District, with broader implications for urban traffic management policies.

title: FusionBots Robotics Curriculum and Textbook

detail.title: FusionBots Robotics Curriculum and Textbook
detail.abstract: This curriculum is a complete, structured program in robotics, engineering, and programming designed to take a student from beginner (elementary school level) to expert (highschool/university level). It is organized into Modules → Units → Lessons, with each lesson containing learning objectives, theoretical content, and hands-on activities/projects. By progressing through all modules and completing the projects and assessments, a dedicated student will gain mastery in mechanical design, electronics, coding (from visual languages to C++/Python), robotics algorithms, artificial intelligence integration with pytorch and tenserflow, and professional engineering practices. This curriculum is aligned with FusionBots' kits and also suggests affordable generic alternatives, ensuring accessibility. The program is scaffolded by age group: younger learners focus on fundamentals and fun exploration, while advanced students tackle rigorous engineering challenges and AI. Throughout, safety and ethics are emphasized to foster responsible innovation.

title: The Impact of The Carbon Emission Trading on the Cleanliness of Corporate Export Products——Evidence from a quasi-natural experiment based on the carbon emission trading pilot
affiliations: Xinjiang University, Northwest Normal University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Xinjiang University and Xinjiang University

detail.title: The Impact of The Carbon Emission Trading on the Cleanliness of Corporate Export Products——Evidence from a quasi-natural experiment based on the carbon emission trading pilot
detail.abstract: Carbon emission trading is an effective market-based means of controlling greenhouse gas emissions, which helps to achieve the goal of "carbon peaking and carbon neutrality". This paper analyzes the impact of the carbon emission trading pilot policy implemented by the Chinese government in 2013 on the cleanliness of Chinese export products. Based on matched data from China's A-share listed companies and China Customs Database, we use a multi-period double-difference method to explore whether and how this policy can enhance the cleanliness of corporate export products. The study finds that the carbon emission trading pilot policy significantly enhances the cleanliness of corporate export products, with robustness verified through parallel trend tests, placebo tests, and PSM-DID methods. The mechanism analysis shows that the carbon emission trading pilot policy affects the cleanliness of corporate export products through two pathways: enhancing the scale of corporate environmental investment and increasing corporate R&D intensity. Further analysis reveals that the effect of the carbon emission trading pilot policy on the cleanliness of corporate export products will be more pronounced when the initial allowances of the carbon emission trading pilot are implemented in a compensated manner, when the baseline method of accounting is adopted, and when the degree of competition in the product market is higher and the pricing power of corporations in the market is relatively lower. In addition, this paper examines the heterogeneity of the impact of the carbon emission trading pilot policy on the cleanliness of corporate export products, considering the nature of corporate property rights, the level of green innovation, and corporate size.

title: Individuals and Nature-Conscious Investment: A Systematic Review and Future Research Agenda
affiliations: University of Limerick - Kemmy Business School, University of Ioannina, University of Limerick - Kemmy Business School and University of Limerick - Kemmy Business School

detail.title: Individuals and Nature-Conscious Investment: A Systematic Review and Future Research Agenda

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the EU Commission HORIZON Programme (Grant No. 101135476).

detail.abstract: Despite the inclusion of biodiversity objectives in sustainable finance taxonomies, their consideration in investment decisions remains limited. This review identifies key behavioural, informational and institutional barriers that inhibit the alignment of individual investment actions with nature-conscious preferences. The literature highlights barriers across several dimensions that result in a misalignment of individuals preferences and actual investment behaviour. These barriers emerge from cognitive biases, financial literacy, information asymmetries as well as structural constraints such as pension system design and implementation. Future research on behavioural interventions, fiduciary responsibility and the integration of biodiversity data in financial labelling and decision-making tools is expected to advance the integration of nature data in investment decisions.
